fundamental.thesis: Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer (Tanishq, CaratLane, Mia; about 8.5% share of organised retail) and also leads in watches (27% analog share) and is the number two organised eyewear chain, with 3,758 stores. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹20,533 cr, up 25.1% YoY, which is faster than the first half overall (H1 ₹41,970 cr, +19.1%, so Q1 was about +13-14%), helped by studded jewellery growing 32%, jewellery same-store growth of 15%, and margin gains in watches (+27% revenue) and eyecare (+28%). However, the H1 PAT of ₹4,170 cr (+88.6%, 9.9% margin) is boosted by one-offs: ₹536 cr of customs duty benefits and a ₹671 cr reduction in the Damas option liability. H1 operating cash flow was negative at -2.68x PAT (FCF -₹11,585 cr), almost certainly from building up gold inventory. Q2 PAT was not extracted, so the latest-quarter margin cannot be confirmed. On valuation, trailing P/E is 74.3x and forward P/E is 49.4x, which sits inside the 60-100x premium band the sector card sets for top consumer franchises, so I grade it fair. The peer screen does show it as expensive (EV/EBITDA 48x vs a 21.9x median, P94), but that peer set is mostly autos and is not a like-for-like comparison. The biggest risks are that jewellery buyer count was flat YoY, so growth depends on bigger ticket sizes and gold prices, and that the earnings are both inflated by one-offs and not yet turning into cash.

fundamental.thesis: TCS is India's largest IT services company (₹8L cr market cap, near-debt-free with filing-reported D/E 0.099 and ROE 51%), serving global clients across BFSI (39.1% of revenue), Manufacturing, and Consumer verticals with dominant scale and 12-year consecutive top-ranked customer satisfaction. Revenue re-accelerated sharply in H1 FY27 to ₹1,45,463 cr (+12.6% YoY, with Q1FY27 at +13.9%), up from a sluggish +4.6% in FY26, and PAT margins expanded from 15.9% in Q3FY26 to 18.8% in H1 FY27 — but the critical flag is that FY26 constant-currency growth was -2.4%, meaning the INR headline re-acceleration is substantially FX-tailwind-driven (INR/USD ~94.96 vs ~84 in FY26) rather than evidence of genuine organic demand recovery; EBITDA margins have also contracted from 28.7% to 27.2%, and deferred revenue declined ₹1,092 cr QoQ, both pointing to margin and pipeline softening beneath the headline beat. At 16.3× trailing P/E — a 33.7% discount to the IT sector peer median of 24.7× and cheapest in sector on forward P/E at 13.4× — TCS screens unambiguously cheap versus both sector peers and the benchmark range of 22–30×, with a pristine balance sheet (CFO/PAT 0.94×, FCF ₹23,768 cr in H1) providing a durable floor; the P/E yardstick is used here as primary per the asset-light IT services model, and EV/EBITDA at 11.1× (P17 in sector vs median 14.7×) corroborates the cheap read. The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

fundamental.thesis: Hindalco is a global aluminium and copper producer: it makes primary aluminium in India, owns Novelis (the world's largest maker of rolled aluminium products) and runs a large copper business, so its earnings swing with LME metal prices. The PAT jump was also helped by about 150 bps from a lower tax rate. For a cyclical, the right yardstick is EV/EBITDA. At 9.3x, Hindalco is cheap against its broad Materials peers (P7, median 17.9x), but that median is pushed up by paint makers. Against the 5–8x mid-cycle range for metal producers, it is somewhat rich for a business near peak LME prices. Trailing P/E of 18.2x sits inside the 12–22x band, forward P/E is 10.3x, and the stock is at 85% of its 52-week range, so overall valuation is fair, not cheap. fundamental.thesis: Bank of Baroda is India's second-largest state-run bank, with about ₹15.1L cr of advances, a growing overseas book (+39.7% YoY) and a government stake of roughly 64%. In Q2FY27, total income rose 19.8% YoY to ₹41,966 cr and PAT rose 35.8% to ₹6,532 cr, a 15.6% margin. That follows a weak Q1FY27 hit by heavy provisions, so H1FY27 profit was still down 16.5%. Loans grew 18.3% and deposits 16.4%, and asset quality improved: gross NPA 1.78%, net NPA 0.37%, provision coverage 94.65%. Profit quality is weaker than the headline: NIM slipped from 2.89% (Q4FY26) to 2.74%, the share of cheap current and savings deposits (CASA) fell three quarters running from 38.9% to 36.37%, fee income fell 8.5% YoY, and treasury gains helped the quarter. I graded valuation on price-to-book plus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, not P/E. At 0.81× book with 12.7% TTM ROE (19.3% annualised in Q2), the stock is cheap: P7 among 15 regional-bank peers on P/B and 6.8× trailing P/E against a peer median of 16.8×. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking as deposits shift to costlier term and overseas FCNR money, which would make the Q2 profit jump look like a one-off driven by treasury gains rather than a steady new level.

fundamental.thesis: Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

In India it ranks #1 in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 companies, growing about 1.27x the Indian pharma market (16.7% vs 13.2%). Growth is speeding up. Revenue growth rose from +14% (Q2FY26) to +20% (Q3FY26) and +25% (Q1FY27), and reached about +32.5% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr, implied from H1 ₹3,420 cr less Q1 ₹1,626 cr). Implied Q2 PAT of ₹388 cr is up about 49%, and PAT margin widened to about 21.6% from 19%, though cash conversion is only moderate (CFO/PAT 0.86x in H1). On the healthcare yardstick of trailing P/E plus peer rank, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28-40x sector band and at P46 vs peers, and forward P/E of 26.3x signals expected earnings growth. The biggest risk is the 29% US generics exposure: generics are tariff-exempt for now, but the pending US Commerce review of generics plus forex losses already hitting reported profit could stall the margin gains, and management has given no forward guidance.

fundamental.thesis: Elgi Equipments is one of India's leading air-compressor makers: compressors bring in about 92% of revenue, and roughly half of sales come from overseas, mainly North America, Europe and Australia. EBITDA margin rose to 16.3% from 14.9% a year ago. Profit grew more slowly: Q2 PAT was about ₹129 cr (H1 ₹232 cr less Q1 ₹103 cr), up only about 6% YoY against +20.7% in Q1, and H1 PAT grew 11.9% against revenue growth of 19.7%. Cash conversion is healthy (CFO/PAT of 1.05x, H1 free cash flow of ₹166 cr). Because this is a business that sells products off the shelf rather than one that works through an order book, I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, with P/E as a cross-check. Great Eastern Shipping is India's largest private shipping company, running crude/product tankers, LPG carriers (VLGCs) and dry-bulk ships, plus an offshore unit; it is tagged Industrials but is really a freight-rate-driven shipping business, so the order-book framework in the sector card does not apply. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹2,234 cr (+61.7% YoY) and PAT ₹1,269 cr (+118.4% YoY, a record), continuing a sharp turnaround from H1FY26 revenue falling -14.7%; PAT margin widened from 39.9% to 56.8% over the window, cash conversion is solid (CFO/PAT about 1.0x), and the company holds ₹8,475 cr net cash at 25% ROCE. For a capital-intensive cyclical I graded on P/B against ROE and on EV/EBITDA rather than P/E: P/B 1.19x with 18.8% ROE and EV/EBITDA 4.69x (P2 in the broad market) make it cheap, and the ongoing buyback below NAV supports that, but low multiples at peak freight rates are typical for shipping and partly price in earnings coming down (forward P/E 7.17x vs trailing 6.86x), even as sell-side EPS estimates were raised +17% in 30 days. The biggest risk is the cycle: Suezmax earnings are up 289% YoY on Hormuz and Black Sea disruptions, only about 58-61% of Q3 tanker and bulk days are fixed, and vessel prices are high, so earnings could fall fast if the geopolitical premium in freight rates fades.

fundamental.thesis: LT Foods is a mid-cap rice-led branded food company, tagged FMCG here, and its most recent extracted numbers are for Q1FY27 because the H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-27 have no figures in the trend table, so the September quarter is unseen. Q1FY27 revenue rose 26.0% YoY to Rs 3,161 cr while PAT rose only 9.0% to Rs 183 cr (5.8% margin), and FY26 showed the same gap with revenue up 26.1% but PAT up just 2.2%; growth has actually held at about 24-26% and the PAT margin slipped modestly from 6.1% (9MFY26) to 5.8%, because the flagged 'decelerating' and 'contracting' signals are distorted by an implausible Q2FY26 row (Rs 277 cr revenue, 59.1% margin) that I excluded, while Q1FY27 volume growth of 12% with 11% price/mix is good but above the 10% level the sector card treats sceptically, gross margin fell from 34.4% to 32.6%, and FY26 cash conversion was solid (CFO/PAT 1.46x, FCF Rs 551 cr). Using P/E against FMCG norms plus EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, valuation grades cheap at 21.5x trailing P/E versus the 40-65x FMCG norm and 10.4x EV/EBITDA (P11, about 55% below the median), though the peer set is the broad market rather than true industry peers, a low multiple in FMCG can signal a structural issue, the 13.3x forward P/E rests on thin coverage of one analyst, and I disregarded the 105% dividend yield and 28.49 debt/equity as likely data errors and the 7.53x P/B because it does not reconcile with the P/E and 14.9% ROE. The biggest risk is that fast sales growth keeps failing to reach profit, a concern reinforced by the 5.5% cut to FY EPS estimates over the last 30 days and the unverified September quarter.

fundamental.thesis: Castrol India is the market-leading branded lubricants company, with a 167,000-outlet distribution network that grew its rural reach to 46,000 outlets, so it behaves more like a consumer-brands business than the oil PSUs in the Energy sector card. For 9M CY26, revenue rose 20.3% YoY to ₹5,151 cr but PAT grew only 8.7% to ₹766 cr; backing out H1 (₹3,417 cr revenue, ₹590 cr PAT) implies the Sep-quarter revenue grew about 27% to roughly ₹1,734 cr while PAT fell about 22% to roughly ₹176 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 18.6% in the Jun quarter to about 10%, and the implied EBITDA margin of about 15% sits well below management's 21-24% target band. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardstick (not the PSU 'policy-priced' P/E-plus-yield framework), the stock trades at 17.7x trailing P/E and 11.9x EV/EBITDA, about 50% below the broad-market median (P18/P17), but trailing earnings include the stronger H1 and FY-EPS estimates were cut 4.9% over 30 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap until margins stabilise. The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

fundamental.thesis: ACME Solar is a renewable power producer with about 2,990 MW running and roughly 5,080 MW under construction, most of it solar, hybrid, firm-and-dispatchable (FDRE) and battery storage (BESS) projects. About 84% of its portfolio sells to central-government buyers on 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs), and it signed a new 400 MW FDRE PPA with NTPC on 30 Oct. Growth is speeding up: revenue rose from +59% in FY26 to +63% in Q1 FY27 and +78% in H1 FY27, reaching ₹1,745 cr, while H1 PAT more than doubled (+105%) to ₹504 cr and PAT margin widened from 19.9% to 28.9%. Implied Q2 revenue was about ₹791 cr against ₹954 cr in Q1, which fits a weaker monsoon quarter for solar, so H1 is the cleaner read. I valued it on EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy power producer. At 15.2x it sits around the 26th percentile of the broad market, and forward P/E of 13.7x versus trailing 40.7x shows strong earnings growth is already expected. On the other side, P/B of 4.0x with ROE of 10.4% is rich, and the stock is at 80% of its 52-week range, so I call it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt is about 3.9x equity, interest costs take about 40% of EBITDA, H1 free cash flow was negative ₹5,263 cr from heavy capex, and grid connection delays (about 6 months on average) could push back commissioning and the earnings it depends on.

fundamental.thesis: HDB Financial Services is a large-scale NBFC and HDFC Bank subsidiary providing retail, commercial vehicle, and enterprise loans across a ₹1.31 lakh crore asset base, with strong parentage constituting its primary competitive moat and funding advantage. Revenue growth has decelerated from a peak of +21.4% (Q3FY26) to +10.3% in H1 FY27 with loan growth similarly slowing from 14.1% to ~11%, while PAT recovered sharply to +36.2% YoY (₹1,565 cr in H1 FY27 vs -2% in H1 FY26) as GNPA improved from 2.81% to 2.43% and Net NPA from 1.34% to 1.09% — partially offset by structurally elevated credit costs (2.58% in FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT -0.34×), which flag earnings quality concerns. Using the P/B+ROE lender yardstick mandated by the sector card, P/B 2.79× against ROE 13.9% places the stock in fair territory (not cheap: P/B > 1.5×; not expensive: P/B < 3× with ROE > 12%); peer-relative ranking at P27 in the broad market and a ~40% discount to sector median P/B, combined with forward P/E 14.7× vs trailing 22.5×, suggest the market has already priced in a meaningful earnings recovery. The primary risk is that loan/AUM growth deceleration (tracking toward low-double-digits) persists in a RISK_OFF macro environment with rising crude costs and an elevated credit cost base, stalling the earnings normalisation that currently drives the bull case.

MRPL is a mid-sized standalone coastal refiner controlled by ONGC, with a small but growing retail fuel network; its profits swing mainly with refining margins (GRM), so the yardstick here is EV/EBITDA alongside a policy-adjusted P/E, not headline growth. Q2 FY27 profit was ₹1,881 cr, up 194% YoY from ₹639 cr. Q2 revenue was not reported directly: subtracting Q1 (₹41,609 cr) from H1 (₹77,199 cr) gives about ₹35,590 cr, roughly +42% YoY and a PAT margin near 5.3%, up from Q1's 2.5% but below Q3 FY26's 4.9% on the trend table's own trajectory flag, which reads margins as volatile and cycle-driven rather than structurally rising. On valuation, EV/EBITDA of 6.0x is in line with a refiner and trailing P/E of 14.5x sits at the top of the 8–14x energy band and above the card's 6–10x PSU refiner norm; the stock screens 'cheap' against the broad market only because no close refining peers were available, and it sits mid-range at 42% of its 52-week band, so we grade it fair. The biggest worry is that sell-side next-year EPS estimates have been cut 21% in 30 days, which suggests the market expects the current strong refining margins to fade. That cut conflicts with the 3.4x forward P/E, which looks like bad data.

fundamental.thesis: Oil India is a state-owned upstream oil and gas producer, and through Numaligarh Refinery it also has refining and a small but growing renewables arm; its earnings mostly track crude prices, production volumes and government policy. The trend data does not add up: the 'H1FY27' row shows revenue of ₹11,915 cr (-33.5% YoY), which is smaller than Q1FY27 alone (₹12,886 cr, +47.3%), so that row is probably Q2 figures mislabelled or a standalone/consolidated mix. If it is Q2, revenue grew about 30% against Q2FY26's ₹9,175 cr and PAT more than doubled from ₹1,044 cr to ₹2,520 cr (21.2% margin), which fits the company's own press release of 20% higher crude output and 116% standalone PAT growth. On the PSU-upstream yardstick from the sector card (P/E 6–10× plus dividend yield), the trailing P/E of 10.3× sits at the top of the band, while the forward P/E of 6.9× and EV/EBITDA of 8.3× look more reasonable, so I grade it fair: priced for policy risk rather than cheap. The broad-market peer ranking (P7) compares it against non-energy stocks and does not count as cheapness. The biggest risks are that earnings depend on crude prices, which could fall or be hit by a windfall tax, and that the company carries about ₹28,800 cr of net debt.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance is India's largest conglomerate and should be read as four businesses: refining and petrochemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (JPL, now separately listed after its 28 Oct 2026 IPO), retail (RRVL) and a new-energy build-out. Q2FY27 revenue rose 27.8% YoY to ₹362,268 cr, up from +24.5% in Q1 and -8.5% in FY26, and PAT rose 33.8% to ₹29,550 cr, a margin of 8.2% (up from 6.8% in Q1, roughly flat against FY26's 8.3%). Most of that came from O2C, where EBITDA jumped 67.9% to ₹25,203 cr on fuel cracks 3–3.7x higher after Middle East supply disruptions; Jio grew steadily (revenue +11.4%, ARPU ₹218.8), but retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%. Using a sum-of-the-parts view with EV/EBITDA as the main multiple, the stock trades at 12.2x EV/EBITDA and 21.7x trailing / 18.0x forward P/E; that looks expensive against the PSU energy median (9.2x P/E), but that comparison is misleading for a conglomerate earning telecom and retail multiples, so I grade it fair. It trades near its 52-week low, has strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.76x) and modest leverage (net debt/EBITDA 0.47x). The biggest risk is that the record quarter depends on crack spreads created by a geopolitical shock, which can reverse quickly while retail and media are weakening.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. On volume, Q2FY27 deposits grew +18.8% YoY and advances grew +16.3%, but profitability is moving the wrong way. Management calls the 3.32% NIM a cycle low, ROA has fallen from 1.9% in FY26 to 1.48% in H1FY27, and H1 PAT of ₹35,869 cr is down -10.2% YoY on revenue down -4.1%, a 14.3% PAT margin. The ₹1,950 cr Q2 PAT figure (+12.7%) looks like an extraction error, and 30-day and 90-day FY EPS estimates have both been cut 5.6%. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, 1.98x book on a 13.8% TTM ROE (12.1% in H1) is fair in absolute terms, but it ranks P79 among bank peers on P/B even though P/E sits at the peer median of 16.8x. The stock is at 8.6% of its 52-week range, which helps the entry but does not make it cheap. The biggest risk is an abrupt leadership change: a new MD/CEO effective immediately and the Deputy MD retiring by December. This comes with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 100%, LCR tight at 113%, and a 25 bps October rate hike that management expects to reprice the 70% floating book upward, which conflicts with the sector card's easing-cycle prior.

fundamental.thesis: Bharti Airtel is the number-two player in India's mobile market, which is now effectively a 2.5-player market, and it leads on premium customers, with growing broadband, enterprise and Africa businesses on top. The extracted Q2 row shows revenue up 16.7% YoY and PAT up 30.8%, with a 14.6% PAT margin and a 57.9% EBITDA margin. However, the absolute figures in that row (Rs 6,088 cr revenue against Rs 21,097 cr in Q4 FY26 and about Rs 2.11L cr for FY26) are clearly not on a like-for-like consolidated basis, so the pre-computed 'decelerating/contracting' trajectory signals are unreliable and I have not relied on them. I graded valuation on the sector card's yardstick, EV/EBITDA: at 10.54x it sits inside the 9-12x norm for Indian mobile, so it is fair. Forward P/E of 21.6x against trailing 40.7x shows earnings growth is expected, and the stock is at only 15% of its 52-week range, which makes the entry better on risk/reward. fundamental.thesis: ITC is a conglomerate: its cigarette business is the main source of cash, alongside growing FMCG, paper, agri and hotel-adjacent businesses, and it is the market leader in Indian cigarettes. In Q2FY27 consolidated net revenue grew only +5.0% YoY, slowing from +27.6% in Q1 on the gross, tax-inclusive line. Q2 PAT was about ₹4,229 cr (H1 ₹8,738 cr minus Q1 ₹4,509 cr), down roughly 16% YoY, the third straight quarter of decline. The main cause is cigarettes: an unprecedented tax increase cut cigarette net revenue by 21% and cigarette profit by 27%, while the non-cigarette businesses grew revenue +20% and EBITDA +22% (FMCG Others +19%, Paper PBIT +48%). On sector-appropriate yardsticks of P/E and EV/EBITDA, the stock looks cheap: 16.9x trailing P/E against an FMCG median of 51.5x (cheapest of 13 peers), 15.8x forward P/E and 12.1x EV/EBITDA, trading at 3% of its 52-week range. The sector card warns that cheap FMCG usually points to a structural problem, and here that problem is the reset in cigarette taxes. The biggest risk is that legal cigarette volumes keep falling and smuggled illicit trade grows, which would cause further earnings downgrades; analysts have already cut FY EPS estimates by 4.8% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: UltraTech is India's largest cement maker with 210.1 mtpa of global grey capacity, and together with Adani it controls about 45% of industry capacity, which supports pricing discipline. fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Unilever is India's largest FMCG company, with leading brands across home care, beauty and personal care, and foods. Revenue growth has picked up sharply over the last few quarters, from +1.9% (9MFY25) to +5% (FY26), +10.1% (Q1FY27) and +14.5% (Q2FY27, ₹18,226 cr). So we cannot tell whether the 14.5% revenue jump is real demand, or price/mix and base effects that are pushing costs up faster than revenue.

fundamental.thesis: Coal India is the state-controlled near-monopoly coal miner that supplies most of India's thermal power fuel, and it earns a steady return from domestic volumes, e-auction premiums and a high dividend payout. In H1 FY27 revenue rose +13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose +18.9% to ₹15,397 cr (PAT margin 17.0%), recovering from a weak FY26 (revenue -0.5%, PAT -12.3%). Cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF ₹26,270 cr). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/E and yield, as the sector card prescribes for PSU energy names. At 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x trailing P/E the stock sits exactly at the Energy peer median (P50) and inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is at 85% of its 52-week range and EPS estimates are drifting slightly lower (-0.9% over 30d), which limits upside. The main risk is that volume growth cannot continue once the inventory buffer is used up while production is still falling, and administered pricing caps any offset from price.

fundamental.thesis: JSW Steel is a large Indian steelmaker that sold a record 7.46 MT in Q2FY27 (+13% YoY), with auto-sector sales up 36%. Revenue growth accelerated from +9.8% in Q1 to +20.6% (₹54,486 cr), and PAT rose 225.6% to ₹5,359 cr, though the YoY figures use a low, restructured base; PAT margin was flat at about 9.8-9.9%, the 'contracting' signal is distorted by FY26's ₹18,051 cr one-off gain, and EBITDA per tonne fell about 11% QoQ from ₹14,990 to ₹13,329 despite rising 24% YoY. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a steel cyclical, the stock is expensive: the reported 12.6x, or roughly 9x on my estimate using annualised Q2 EBITDA and net debt, is above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, and the 13.8x trailing P/E and 'cheap vs peers' verdict carry little weight because of the one-off gain and a peer set that includes paint and adhesive companies. The biggest risk is that steel spreads narrow from here, with the stock at 92% of its 52-week range and EBITDA per tonne already falling sequentially, leaving little room for error.

fundamental.thesis: Divi's Laboratories is one of India's largest API and custom-synthesis (CDMO) manufacturers, near debt-free (D/E 0.04), with a clean FDA note in the latest filing and a tailwind from China+1 sourcing and a weaker rupee. Q1 FY27 revenue rose 27.8% YoY to ₹3,080 cr and PAT rose 65.5% to ₹902 cr (29.3% PAT margin, EBITDA margin 42.8%), a sharp step-up from roughly +12-15% revenue growth through FY26 (FY26: ₹10,560 cr, +12.8%), though Q4 FY26 data is missing and management itself calls the business lumpy and guides only 'double-digit' growth with full-year gross margin near 60% versus Q1's ~68%. On the CDMO yardstick of EV/EBITDA, cross-checked with P/E, the stock is expensive: EV/EBITDA is 49.9x against a peer median of 21.4x (P92), and trailing P/E is 68.2x against the 28-40x pharma benchmark (P85 vs peers), while forward P/E of 46.9x still prices in strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that Q1 was a lumpy peak quarter; if Q2 results on 7 Nov show margins normalising toward guidance, a multiple this rich leaves little room for disappointment.

Grasim is a diversified Aditya Birla holding company: it controls UltraTech (cement), Aditya Birla Capital (lending) and renewables, and runs its own businesses in cellulosic fibre, caustic chemicals, Birla Opus paints and the Birla Pivot B2B e-commerce platform. In Q2 FY27, consolidated revenue rose 26.0% YoY to ₹50,105 cr, up from +21.4% in Q1. Cement volumes grew 12.9%, the lending book grew 32%, Opus revenue grew 35% and Pivot grew 66%. But owners took a ₹234 cr loss (-0.5% PAT margin), mainly from a ₹767 cr one-off charge for idling the Canadian pulp mill (AVNB). EBITDA margin also fell from 23.5% in Q1 to 13.0%, so profit is not keeping up with revenue. Because Grasim is a capital-heavy holding company, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/B with ROE rather than trailing P/E (42.4×, inflated by depressed earnings). EV/EBITDA of 13.2× is 26% below the Materials median (P27) and P/B of 2.1× is at P19, but ROE is only 6.3% and the stock sits at 87% of its 52-week range, so overall it is fair, not cheap. The forward P/E of 21.2× already assumes a strong earnings recovery. The main risk is that paints keeps losing money and leverage keeps rising (debt/equity 1.43×, H1 FCF of -₹22,342 cr, ₹17,200 cr renewables acquisition pending), which would keep consolidated ROE low and keep the holding-company discount wide.

fundamental.thesis: TMPV is Tata Motors' passenger-vehicle business after the demerger. Most of its revenue and profit comes from JLR (Range Rover, Defender, Jaguar), and the rest from Tata's domestic PV and EV range, where it is a leading EV maker with about 14% EV mix. Q2FY27 revenue rose 33.9% YoY to ₹96,920 cr, but that jump mostly reflects a weak base, because JLR was hit by a cyber incident in Q2FY26; revenue grew only about 1% over Q1FY27's ₹95,799 cr, and Q1 itself grew just 9.3% YoY. EBITDA margin has fallen for two quarters in a row (9.4% → 7.4% → 5.5%) on adverse mix and rising commodity costs, and PAT swung to a ₹5,451 cr loss (-5.6% margin) after ₹6,738 cr of restructuring charges (₹3,776 cr employee separation plus ₹2,856 cr impairments). Trailing P/E is not meaningful because earnings are negative, so I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy carmaker: 7.1x against a peer median of 18.3x, with P/B of 1.3x and forward P/E of 7.2x, all the cheapest among its auto peers. That makes it cheap, though a JLR-heavy, cyclical, leveraged business deserves part of that discount. The biggest risks are the balance sheet and earnings estimates: net debt has risen to ₹50.8K cr, free cash flow is negative, interest coverage is only 1.3x, and analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 22% in the last 30 days, so the low multiple may be pricing in further earnings cuts rather than a real bargain.

Using the sector card's P/E-plus-yield yardstick for oil marketers, valuation is fair rather than cheap: the 4.71x trailing P/E and 3.74x EV/EBITDA are below the peer medians of 9.2x and 6.1x, but the P/E appears to reflect older, peak earnings, since our rough trailing-12-month PAT of ₹15,800 cr implies about 7.6x, in line with the 7.19x forward P/E and inside the 6-10x policy-priced range, and the 678% dividend yield is a clear data error so yield could not be assessed. The biggest risk is that crude at $104 and rising squeezes marketing margins if retail fuel prices stay frozen, at a time when H1 free cash flow was -₹12,440 cr and CFO/PAT was -1.00x.

Eicher Motors owns Royal Enfield, the clear leader in India's premium motorcycle market with about 87% domestic share in its segment, and also holds 50% of the VECV commercial-vehicle joint venture, which added ₹354 cr to H1 FY27 profit. Q2 FY27 alone (H1 minus Q1) shows revenue of about ₹7,422 cr, up +20.3% YoY, and PAT of about ₹1,573 cr, up +14.9% YoY. fundamental.thesis: Kaynes Technology is a mid-cap electronics contract manufacturer (EMS) expanding into chip packaging (OSAT), PCBs and, through a newly signed joint venture with Toyokawa Techno, display modules, which puts it in line with the China+1 and PLI themes. Because this business needs heavy capital spending, I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA: 39× is about 68% above the broad-market median of 23×, and trailing P/E of 68× is in the 82nd percentile. That is expensive for a company whose profits are not turning into cash, even with the stock at 11% of its 52-week range and analysts cutting FY EPS estimates by 13% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the restatements and fast-growing receivables and inventory mean reported profits overstate the cash the business really earns, which could push the stock lower still.

The biggest risk is that claims inflation in motor and health keeps the combined ratio above 105% and the expected rebound never arrives, which would leave little room to justify the premium multiple.

On the fallback multiples LIC is the cheapest of its 4 life-insurance peers on every measure: trailing P/E 8.7x vs a peer median of 53.7x, P/B 2.0x vs 6.8x. The biggest risk is that LIC keeps losing new-business share to private insurers while margins on that business stay low, and without VNB/APE data this cannot be checked. fundamental.thesis: Niva Bupa is a standalone health insurer with about 11% of India's retail health market, 27 million lives covered, and a growing agency, branch and bank-partner network. Using P/B against ROE as the yardstick for an insurer (P/E is distorted by the FY26 Ind-AS transition), the stock looks fair to slightly rich: P/B of 3.84x for an ROE of only 12.1% is demanding. So 'fair' is a better grade than the 'expensive' implied by the 75x trailing P/E. The biggest risk is claims inflation or a worse claims mix as fast retail growth seasons, which would push a combined ratio already near 100% above it.

For a lender we value on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE), not P/E: P/B is 1.7x against an annualised H1FY27 ROE of 15.2%, up from about 7% trailing. That is fair to slightly cheap (P13 on P/B, forward P/E 11x), but the stock sits at 86% of its 52-week range, so the rebound is mostly priced in. The biggest risk is falling gold prices: AUM grew about 92% while gold tonnage grew only 22%, so loans per gram of gold have risen, collateral cover is thinner and auction losses could rise. Q2 asset-quality figures were also not disclosed.

fundamental.thesis: PB Fintech runs Policybazaar and Paisabazaar, India's largest online marketplaces for insurance and credit. It earns commissions and does not lend, so the lender yardsticks in the Financials sector card (P/B plus ROE) do not fit, and the debt/equity figure of 4.92 is probably a data artefact, not real leverage. The latest quarter we can verify, Q1FY27, had revenue of ₹1,888 cr, up 40.0% year on year, faster than +37.0% in Q3FY26 and +36.5% for FY26 as a whole. PAT was ₹163 cr, up 92%, but PAT margin has slipped from 10.7% to 9.9% to 8.6% and EBITDA margin from 11.2% to 7.4%, so growth is costing more margin than before. Q2FY27 numbers have not been extracted from the filed results; the yfinance figure of ₹773 cr revenue does not match a ₹1,888 cr Q1 run-rate, so it was ignored. Judged as a high-growth platform on price-to-sales and growth, the stock looks expensive: P/S is 11.0x, EV/EBITDA is 140.6x (99th percentile of the broad market), trailing P/E is 111x and forward P/E is 47.8x (91st percentile). That is a full price even for ~40% growth, while next-year earnings estimates have been cut 15.1% over 90 days and 7.9% over 30 days. The biggest risk is that the premium multiple shrinks if margins keep falling while analysts keep cutting estimates.

fundamental.thesis: Star Health is a health-focused insurer, with ₹9,635 cr of H1 FY27 revenue from its health segment (up 13%) out of ₹10,856 cr in total. H1 FY27 revenue rose 10.4% to ₹10,856 cr and PAT rose 57.3% to ₹815 cr, but the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' trend signals are unreliable because they mix H1, Q1, 9M and full-year periods across an Ind AS restatement; underlying profitability looks weaker, with PAT falling from ₹550 cr in Q1 to an implied ₹265 cr in Q2, the combined operating ratio worsening from 92.33% to 94.52%, and the claims ratio at 68.95%. Using P/B against ROE as the closest available yardstick (the sector card names none for general insurers and the peer set is only a broad-market fallback), valuation is expensive at 3.32x book for a 7.5% ROE, although a forward P/E of 20.4x versus a trailing 50.48x and FY EPS estimates up 6.7% in 30 days show the market expects a sharp earnings recovery; the price input also needs checking, because the consensus upside implies about ₹511 while market cap and the 52-week position imply about ₹572. The biggest risk is that this recovery fails to arrive if underwriting keeps weakening, and earnings quality is already a concern with operating cash flow down 54% to ₹611 cr, CFO/PAT at 0.75x, and the reported ₹40,000 cr NCD redemption looking like an extraction error since it exceeds the ₹33,654 cr market cap.

Revenue fell 6.3% YoY to ₹2,906 cr in Q2 FY27, better than Q1's -20.2%, but growth has slid from +3.4% in H1 FY26 to -16.6% in H1 FY27, and PAT margin has shrunk from 3.7% to about 1.4% (Q2 PAT ₹41 cr, down 61%); H1 operating cash flow was negative ₹340 cr with free cash flow of about -₹1,047 cr. The one bright spot is order intake: ₹15,968 cr won in H1 against ₹4,125 cr in all of FY26, lifting the order book to ₹43,837 cr, about 4x trailing revenue (my calculation; the feed's 15x figure looks wrong). On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a contractor: 12.1x is cheap against the broad market (P18), but a 4.7% ROE does not justify 2.15x book and trailing P/E of 46.9x is at the top of the industrials range, so I grade it fair; the biggest risk is that the new orders do not turn into revenue and cash fast enough while arbitration claims (about ₹838 cr contested) and interest coverage of only 2.2x strain the balance sheet, a concern backed by sell-side earnings estimates being cut 10-14% over the last 30-90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Aditya Infotech sells video-surveillance and security products under the CP PLUS brand, a leading name in India, and makes its own hardware through the AIL Dixon manufacturing joint venture. It is a product and distribution business, not an order-book contractor, so the usual Industrials order-book measures do not apply. The filings only give the latest period as a half-year (the data table labels it H1FY26, but the QIP and fire dates in the notes put it in H1 FY27, the half ended September 2026). In that half, revenue rose 89.7% YoY to ₹3,148 cr and PAT rose 218% to ₹328 cr, a 10.4% PAT margin and 16.4% EBITDA margin, even after a ₹34 cr exceptional fire loss. Two caveats: the table's 'accelerating/expanding' trajectory labels look wrong because the period labels are mislabeled and inconsistent, and the profits are not turning into cash (operating cash flow was -₹67 cr, CFO/PAT -0.20x, free cash flow -₹180 cr, as inventory and receivables piled up). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E. The stock is clearly expensive: trailing P/E of 109.5x against the 28–45x Industrials range, EV/EBITDA of 70x, forward P/E still 51x, around the 95th percentile of the broad market on every multiple, and trading at 92.6% of its 52-week range. Rising analyst estimates (+12% over 90 days) support the growth story, but the average target price is only about 4% above the current price. The biggest risks are a de-rating if the cash drain continues while growth slows, plus a ₹308.6 cr customs penalty still under CESTAT appeal.

fundamental.thesis: Finolex Cables is a mid-cap maker of electrical wires and cables (about 88% of revenue) and optical fibre cables (about 9%), and is adding fibre-draw and preform capacity. In Q1 FY27, revenue was ₹2,013 cr (+44.2% YoY) and PAT was ₹249 cr (+53.1% YoY, 12.4% margin). Growth has sped up from +5.0% in Q2 FY26 to +19.0% in Q4 FY26 to +44.2%, and an unlabelled latest row (₹2,269 cr revenue, ₹286 cr PAT, probably Q2 FY27) suggests it held up. Much of that growth comes from copper-linked price hikes rather than volume: there were 14 price increases in FY26, about 24.5% effective electrical price inflation, and only about 7% wire volume growth in Q1. Other income was about ₹237 cr in FY26, which lifts reported PAT. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the capital-goods yardstick named in the sector card: at 22.8x it sits right at the broad-market median (P49). Trailing P/E of 24.8x and forward P/E of 17.1x look cheaper, but the stock is at 95% of its 52-week range and analysts have been raising estimates (+4.8% FY, +7.5% next-FY), so I call it fair. The biggest risk is that a copper price reversal or weak building-wire and agri-cable volumes cuts both the revenue growth and the gains on a ₹300 cr inventory build.

Sammaan Capital (formerly Indiabulls Housing Finance) is a mid-sized housing and mortgage NBFC that is resetting its business after International Holding Company (Abu Dhabi) became promoter in March 2026 with ₹8,850 cr of committed capital, which lifted its ratings to AA+. H1 FY27 revenue fell 24.3% YoY to ₹3,534 cr and PAT fell 13.6% to ₹556 cr. The implied Q2 alone (H1 minus Q1) was revenue of about ₹1,851 cr, down about 18% YoY, and PAT of about ₹313 cr, roughly flat YoY, so the decline is easing from Q1's -30% revenue and -27% PAT, though interest income is still contracting (-25.7% for H1). On the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE, not P/E), the stock trades at 0.75x book, at the P1 percentile of the broad market. That looks cheap at first glance, but trailing ROE is -35% because of the FY26 ₹6,499 cr exceptional write-down on reclassified non-core loans, and annualised H1 earnings imply only about 4% ROE on a roughly ₹26,600 cr book. A discount to book is therefore fair, not a clear mispricing, until profitability rebuilds. The main risk is that the loan book cannot be regrown profitably enough to lift ROE into double digits. The low 0.16% gross NPA comes after the bad loans were moved out of the book, so it says little about the credit quality of new lending.

fundamental.thesis: Gallantt Ispat is an integrated long-steel maker with captive power and a pellet plant, and it claims about 25% share in its addressable regions; it behaves like a steel-spread business rather than an order-book Industrials name, so EBITDA per tonne matters more than the sector card's order-book metrics. Revenue growth improved from +1.6% in Q1 FY27 to +13.1% in Q2 (Rs 1,146 cr), but PAT fell 30.4% YoY to Rs 61 cr, PAT margin dropped from 10.8% to 5.3% in one quarter, EBITDA margin fell from 17.8% to 9.6%, and H1 cash conversion weakened to 0.49x CFO/PAT with FCF of Rs -188 cr. EV/EBITDA, the preferred yardstick here, is unavailable, so on P/E and P/B I grade the stock expensive: the 36.9x trailing P/E is above the 12-22x Materials range, appears to reflect FY26 PAT of about Rs 484 cr, and is closer to 44x on my estimate of trailing-twelve-month PAT (about Rs 406 cr), while P/B is 5.4x and the broad-market peer rank (P53) is a weak comparison because it has no true steel peers. The biggest risk is that the price assumes a margin recovery while costs are rising, utilisation is stuck at 70% and a Rs 3,000 cr capex plan is absorbing cash; identical Rs 1,146 cr revenue in Q1 and Q2, a volume decline implied by the EBITDA figures despite 13% revenue growth, and the 14% dividend yield also need checking against the source filings, which limits conviction.

fundamental.thesis: Godrej Industries is a holding company for the Godrej group. It runs its own chemicals business and controls Godrej Properties (real estate), Godrej Agrovet (animal feed, veg oils, dairy, crop care) and a growing lending arm. Its 'Industrials' tag fits poorly, so the industrials order-book KPIs do not apply. Revenue growth sped up from about +5% YoY through FY26 to +22.2% in Q1FY27 (₹5,448 cr), led by veg oils (+42.8%), finance (+43.5%) and chemicals (+31.4%). But profit went the other way: PAT to owners fell 36.5% YoY to ₹239 cr, PAT margin dropped from 7.8% to 4.4%, and real-estate revenue fell 17.5%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a leveraged, capital-heavy group. At 23.8× it sits almost exactly at the broad-market median (23.3×, P51), and trailing P/E of 32.1× (P45) and P/B of 3.4× (P38) are also mid-pack. With the stock at 54% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest worry is the balance sheet: gross debt/equity rose from 1.90× to 2.38×, and FY26 free cash flow was about -₹9,883 cr. Q2FY27 results are due on 13 Nov 2026, and the current numbers are one quarter stale.

Godawari Power & Ispat is an integrated mid-cap steel maker (captive iron ore mining, pellets, sponge iron, steel and captive power) that is now spending heavily to diversify into battery energy storage through its subsidiary GNEPL. Earnings are shrinking: H1FY27 profit before tax fell 19.0% YoY, from Rs 514 cr to Rs 417 cr, after 9MFY26 PAT was already down 11.2% on revenue of -3.5%. Q3FY26 revenue fell 11.4% and PAT margin dropped to 12.3%, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates 19.1% over 90 days. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the better measure for a capital-heavy materials business, and chose that and the Materials benchmark over the Industrials sector card because the business is materials. At 13.5x EV/EBITDA and 19.5x trailing P/E it sits inside the Materials range of 12-22x, so I rate it fair. fundamental.thesis: Hitachi Energy India (POWERINDIA) is the dominant T&D equipment manufacturer in India — transformers, HVDC systems, GIS switchgear, grid automation — positioned at the epicentre of India's ₹9 lakh cr power-transmission buildout to 2032, with a first-mover edge in HVDC and BESS. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated to +68.6% YoY (₹2,494 cr vs ₹1,479 cr in Q1FY26), and PAT grew 123.5% YoY to ₹294 cr; EBITDA margins have expanded from 10.0% in FY25 to 16.0% in Q1FY27, supported by a record ₹32,222 cr order book (3.23× annualised revenue cover = 13+ quarters visibility) — a structurally strong and accelerating fundamental picture. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for this capital-intensive industrial (per sector card yardstick), the stock trades at 91× EV/EBITDA and 120× trailing P/E — P96–P98 versus all listed peers and well above the sector card's richest comparable range of 50–80× for T&D electricals — making the stock unambiguously expensive even after accounting for the quality premium and earnings ramp visible in the 62× forward P/E. The central risk is that 91× EV/EBITDA prices in multi-year flawless execution, and the sector card explicitly flags 30–50% de-ratings on capex-pause fears before earnings slow — a scenario now amplified by Q1FY27's 55% YoY collapse in order inflows (base-effect distorted but still real), ₹4,000 cr incremental capex lifting D/E to 1.66×, and surging FX/commodity losses of ₹60 cr.

MMTC is a government-owned trading company, tagged Industrials, whose core trading business has nearly stopped: H1 FY27 operating revenue was only Rs 1.95 cr. Almost all of its earnings now come from interest on its roughly Rs 1,926 cr net cash and Rs 111.48 cr of dividend income. Operating revenue fell 20.7% YoY, down from +12.9% growth in Q3 FY26, and consolidated PAT fell 42.1% YoY to Rs 124.41 cr from Rs 215.07 cr, mostly because last year's Rs 378 cr exceptional gain did not repeat. Operating cash flow was negative Rs 179 cr (CFO/PAT -1.44x), so reported profit is not turning into cash. The sector card's order-book test does not fit a company with no order book, so I graded value on cash backing and earnings quality: a trailing P/E of 29x looks fair against the market median of 35.2x (P39), but the Rs 11,242 cr market cap is about 5.8x net cash and 3,297x sales, at 88% of the 52-week range, so the price is expensive for earnings that are mostly treasury income. The biggest risk to the thesis is that no operating business is generating profit, while the Anglo Coal litigation (Rs 82.82 cr unprovided, flagged in a qualified audit opinion) and the subsidiary fraud cases keep governance and contingent-liability risk high.

The biggest risk is that the export recovery (Bangladesh coaches from Q3 FY27) or the conversion of the order book into revenue keeps slipping. fundamental.thesis: Waaree Energies is India's largest solar module maker. The positives are that management held its FY27 operating EBITDA guidance of ₹7,000–7,700 cr, cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 2.1x, net cash ₹3,224 cr) and the order book of ₹59,200 cr covers 2.2x revenue. The biggest risk is a global module glut (utilisation fell to 45% from 71%) combined with US Section 232 and AD/CVD duties, which cut the overseas mix from 47% to 18.5%. Together these could keep pushing margins and the multiple lower.

Usha Martin is one of the world's larger wire-rope makers, selling specialty ropes to oil and gas, mining, cranes and infrastructure customers, and it gets a meaningful share of revenue from exports. Revenue growth has picked up: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹2,021 cr, up 14.8%, against about 5–6% through FY26. Taking H1 minus Q1, Q2 revenue was about ₹988 cr, up roughly 13% YoY. Profit growth is slowing sharply, though: PAT rose 40.9% in Q1 but only 5.9% to ₹136 cr in Q2, so the Q2 PAT margin fell to about 13.7% from about 14.7% a year ago, even though the table's trajectory signal reads 'expanding'. On valuation, EV/EBITDA is 19.4x, about 17% below the broad-market median of 23.3x and around the 40th percentile. Trailing P/E is 28.3x, at the low end of the 28–45x range for Industrials, and forward P/E falls to 21.2x. That makes the stock fair rather than cheap, especially at 77% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that Q2's slowdown in profit growth, along with weaker cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT of 0.78x against 1.42x in FY26), points to cost or working-capital pressure. fundamental.thesis: Linde India is a subsidiary of the global Linde group that makes industrial gases and also runs a lower-margin project engineering arm. In short, sales are growing faster but that growth is not reaching profit, and heavy capex (about 96% of H1 revenue) pushed free cash flow to -₹647 cr. Industrial gases is a utility-like business, not a steel or cement cyclical, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and peer multiples. Deepak Fertilisers is an integrated ammonia-based chemicals and fertiliser maker that leads several of its niches: about 60% market share in concentrated nitric acid, 40% in technical ammonium nitrate (TAN) and 38% in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) in West India. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 10.9% YoY to ₹3,334 cr, a bit slower than the +12.0% for FY26, but profit grew far faster. PAT rose 83.9% to ₹394 cr, so PAT margin went from 6.4% in FY26 to 11.8%, and EBITDA margin rose 706 bps to 22.5%. This came from Chemicals revenue (+42.5%) and the Equinor gas contract, with strong cash backing (CFO/PAT 3.3x, FCF ₹542 cr). Crop Nutrition revenue fell 12.8%. This is a capital-intensive cyclical, so I graded it on EV/EBITDA. At 11.1x it is above the sector card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for chemicals cyclicals, while trailing P/E of 16.9x sits inside the 12–22x Materials range and forward P/E of 10.6x already prices in more growth. So the verdict is fair, not cheap. The broad-market peer discount compares it with unrelated sectors and I gave it little weight. The biggest risk is that the margin jump depends on gas-cost and IPA pricing that may not last, while fertiliser margins face phosphoric acid shortages and raw-material inflation, and the Dahej and Gopalpur projects (98% complete) still have to start up on time in Q4FY27.

On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive chemicals business, the stock trades at 34.6× against 5–8× for mid-cycle chemical cyclicals, alongside 56× trailing P/E, 38.8× forward P/E and around P75–P79 across all four peer metrics; with the price at 93% of its 52-week range, it is expensive even after strong upward EPS revisions (+22.6% over 90 days). The biggest risk is that refrigerant-gas prices come off their cycle high while ₹319 cr of half-year capex and ₹1,070 cr of net debt are still ramping, which would squeeze margins on a valuation that leaves no room for a miss.

NMDC Steel runs a single 3 MTPA integrated steel plant at Nagarnar that was demerged from NMDC Ltd; the government holds 50.79% and a strategic sale is still pending, so it is a young, single-asset mill still ramping up. In Q1FY27 revenue was ₹3,662 cr, up 8.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹51 cr, a 1.4% margin. EBITDA margin has climbed from -37.9% in Q3FY25 and -20.2% in FY25 to 12.1%, so the turnaround is real. But revenue growth has slowed sharply from triple digits to under 9%, and profits are only just above zero. Steel mills are capital-intensive, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names. At 11.7x it sits well above the 5-8x mid-cycle range for steel, so the stock looks expensive. The P/E of 236x and the P/B of 1.05x both reflect an ROE of only 0.4%, so neither means much yet. The board approved Q2FY27 results on 2026-11-12, but those numbers have not been extracted yet, so this view rests on stale Q1 data and the new quarter could change it in either direction.

fundamental.thesis: Aster DM Healthcare runs multi-specialty hospitals in India and, after its merger with Quality Care (CARE Hospitals) took effect on 1 July 2026, has about 10,840 beds across 27 cities, making it one of the larger listed hospital chains. In Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹2,829 cr, up 19% YoY, and normalised PAT was ₹281 cr, up 34%, giving a PAT margin of about 9.9%; for H1 FY27, revenue was ₹5,429 cr (+20%) and normalised PAT ₹457 cr (+27%). Occupancy rose 335 bps to 68% and patient volumes grew 12%, so the growth looks real, though the YoY figures may be on a merger-combined basis and the normalised PAT leaves out integration costs. The pre-computed signal calls revenue 'accelerating', but +20% to +19% is a slight slowdown, and it compares a half-year with a quarter, so it is not a clean trend. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy hospital business: at 45.9x (P87 vs the broad market, about 97% above the median), a trailing P/E of 123x, P/B of 8.9x against ROE of only 10.1%, and the stock at 85% of its 52-week range, it is expensive. The biggest risk is that analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by about 18% in the last 30 days while all 12 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating, on top of heavy capex (₹1,200+ cr over 18 months, 4,230 new beds planned by FY30) and the risk of merger synergies falling short.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC is India's largest iron-ore miner and a state-run commodity producer, so it takes global prices rather than setting them. It should be judged on cost position and balance sheet, not on a consumer-style multiple. Growth has nearly stopped. Revenue growth slowed from +27.0% in H1FY26 and +33.3% in FY26 to +0.8% in Q1FY27 and +2.4% in H1FY27 (₹13,433 cr). H1 PAT was flat at ₹3,645 cr (-0.6% YoY), and H1 EBITDA fell 15.3% YoY to ₹4,712 cr as royalty and levies rose. Taking H1 minus Q1, Q2FY27 alone was about ₹6,638 cr revenue (roughly +4% YoY) and ₹1,669 cr PAT (roughly -2% YoY), a PAT margin of about 25.1%, down from 29.1% in Q1. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a commodity miner, NMDC trades at 7.8×, the top end of the 5–8× mid-cycle range, so the stock is fair rather than a bargain, even though its 10.45× trailing P/E sits below the 12–22× Materials benchmark. The broad-market peer rank (P6–P7) is not a like-for-like comparison, and the 52-week position is mid-range (71%). The biggest risks sit off the income statement: a ₹16,189 cr Karnataka mineral-tax contingent liability, which is about 2.2× FY26 PAT (not 53% as the pack says), and about ₹10,500 cr owed by the financially weak NMDC Steel and RINL. Cash conversion is also mediocre at 0.66–0.83× CFO/PAT.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant Pharmova is a US-focused specialty pharma group (79% of revenue from the USA, 95% in USD) spanning radiopharmaceuticals, allergy immunotherapy, CDMO sterile injectables, CRDMO and generics. fundamental.thesis: Max Healthcare is one of India's largest listed hospital chains, with about 6,100 network beds running at more than 75% occupancy. It is growing by adding beds at existing hospitals and buying new ones (Kalinga in Bhubaneswar, a land parcel in Pune, 85 more beds at its Noida hospital). But revenue growth has slowed from above 30% to about 17–20%, and H1 PAT fell 7.7% YoY to ₹737 cr. Most of that fall comes from the tax rate going back to normal: it rose from an unusually low 5.6% to 24.5% because of a one-off merger-related tax reversal last year. Cash generation is solid, with operating cash flow at 1.35x PAT and ₹406 cr of free cash flow in H1. The biggest risk is that analysts keep cutting their EPS estimates (down 4.5% over 90 days) while capex for new beds and acquisitions stays heavy. NATCO Pharma is a niche-generics maker whose profits have depended heavily on limited-competition US launches, mainly generic Revlimid (lenalidomide). It also runs smaller businesses in Indian formulations, APIs and crop health, and owns 49% of Adcock Ingram in South Africa. The Revlimid windfall is now running off. Q2FY27 revenue fell 30.4% YoY to ₹1,019cr and PAT fell 60.9% to ₹203cr. PAT margin shrank from 42.6% in FY25 and 34.8% in FY26 to 19.9%, and international formulations fell 41.4%. Domestic pharma grew 38.2% and revenue rose 28% from Q1, so there are some offsets. Trailing P/E of 11.2x and EV/EBITDA of 9.6x look very cheap against the 28–40x pharma range, but they include the windfall. Following the sector card, I graded on run-rate earnings instead: Q2 PAT × 4 is about ₹810cr, or roughly 19.5x market cap, and forward P/E is 19.3x. That is below the sector range, but a business with shrinking earnings deserves a discount, so I call it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the new businesses and Adcock cannot fill the earnings gap. Cash conversion is weak: H1 CFO is only ₹61cr, CFO/PAT is 0.30x and FCF is ₹-215cr, while capex, the Adcock purchase and a ₹750/share rights issue all draw on capital.

Amber Enterprises makes room-AC components and electronics (PCBs) on contract for consumer-durables brands, and is spending heavily on acquisitions (Ascent, Power-One, Unitronics, Stelltek) to grow its electronics, railway and defence businesses. In Q2 FY27 revenue rose 59.5% YoY to ₹2,627 cr from ₹1,647 cr, up from +7.9% growth in Q1 FY27. But the company lost ₹66 cr (PAT margin -2.5%), more than double the ₹32 cr loss a year ago, and PAT margin fell from 2.5% in Q1 to -2.5%. Q2 is the AC off-season, and a fire at the IL JIN plant (since back in operation) hurt the quarter, but sales growth is still not turning into profit. Measured on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy contract manufacturer, it trades at 32.7× against a peer median of 23.3× (69th percentile), and trailing P/E is 159× (99th percentile, above even the sector's usual 60–100× premium band), so we grade it expensive. Forward P/E of 41.9× still assumes a sharp earnings recovery, yet analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by 26% in the last 30 days. Short-term borrowings more than doubled in six months, from ₹145 cr to ₹316 cr, to fund the deals and capex.

I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for this capital-intensive manufacturer: 39.5x sits at the 82nd percentile of the broad market, and trailing P/E of 81.7x is at the 88th percentile, against an ROE of only 6.7% on a P/B of 5.3x, so it is expensive. The forward P/E of 34x prices in a sharp earnings rebound, but sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 6% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that thin margins, debt-funded capex and a crude/INR cost squeeze in a risk-off market delay that rebound and trigger a de-rating.

trader.reasoning: All three analysts lean positive. But the evidence for buying today is weak. The growth figures are unreliable (some half-year and quarterly rows are mixed up). The fundamental data puts the 52-week high at ₹1,250 and the consensus target near ₹1,524, both well below today's ₹1,641 close, so either the price has already run past the targets or the data is off. fundamental.thesis: PVR INOX is a leading Indian multiplex operator whose results depend on film releases and cinema footfall, and it sold its Zea Maize food business in January 2026. H1 FY27 PAT was Rs 320 cr vs Rs 106 cr in the H1 FY26 row (about +202%, not the +526% shown), and implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 264 cr matches yfinance's Rs 263 cr, but the growth trend is unreliable: H1 revenue of Rs 2,717 cr (shown as -21.2%) is -17.5% against Rs 3,292 cr, its 8.4% PAT margin implies about Rs 3,800 cr (+16%), and the 'decelerating revenue' and 'expanding margin' signals mix H1 and quarterly rows, with Q1 FY26 revenue of Rs 147 cr looking like a 10x error, so Q1 FY27's +11.9% is the last usable growth figure. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive, lease-heavy business, 7.41x (P6 vs a broad-market peer set, not cinema peers) with P/B of 1.27x and a price at 14% of the 52-week range grades cheap, with modest confidence because the 53.06x trailing P/E appears to exclude H1 FY27 profit, the 16.16x forward P/E needs earnings to roughly triple, ROE is only 2.4%, and the consensus '+7.7% upside' implies a price near Rs 1,524, well above the Rs 1,250 52-week high. The biggest risks are that a weak film slate hits a high fixed-cost business and that the recovery proves less durable than the +27.6% estimate upgrades suggest; separately, the promoter's Regulation 31 disclosure dated 2026-11-03 needs checking for any share pledge, and no footfall, ticket-price or management guidance data was available.

IRCTC is the state-backed monopoly for online rail ticketing, onboard and station catering, Rail Neer bottled water and rail tourism, and it sits on about ₹3,782 cr of net cash. Revenue growth has sped up from +3.8% (Q1FY26) to +11.6% (FY26), +18.1% (Q1FY27) and +17.2% for H1FY27 (₹2,703 cr), which implies about ₹1,333 cr and roughly +16% for Q2FY27; profit has not kept pace, with H1 PBT down 11.3% to ₹798 cr. Even after adding back the one-off ₹116 cr GST tribunal provision, PBT was only about +1.6% YoY, because the growth came from low-margin catering (+30%, 9.6% margin) and tourism (+21%, 9.1% margin), while the 82%-margin internet ticketing business grew just 0.8%. On valuation I used P/E and EV/EBITDA, which suit this asset-light business better than the sector card's 60-100x premium-retail norms: a trailing P/E of 30.1x (P41 vs the broad market), forward P/E of 23.0x and EV/EBITDA of 23.4x (P50) make it fair, and the stock near its 52-week low (10% of the range) makes entry better, but analysts have cut EPS estimates by about 9% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the ticketing profit engine has stopped growing while new revenue arrives at much lower margins, plus Rail Neer losses and an unresolved licence-fee dispute (Delhi HC hearing January 2027).

No material company-specific news (FinBERT data missing, only price chatter), and Consumer Discr. sector flows are neutral, so neither changes the read.

fundamental.thesis: Physicswallah is a fast-growing Indian test-prep and edtech company that sells online courses and runs a growing chain of offline coaching centres. Note that yfinance tags it FMCG, which is wrong; it belongs under Consumer Discretionary. On the latest quarter we could verify from filings (Q1 FY27), revenue was about ₹1,054 cr, up 24.4% YoY. That is slower than the 35.0% growth for full-year FY26, and EBITDA margin fell from 14.1% (FY26) to 4.9% in Q1, while FY26 PAT was a ₹24 cr loss. The Q2 FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-04 but have not been extracted into our trend table. The unverified yfinance Q2 figures (₹738 cr revenue, ₹144 cr PAT) cannot be relied on, and the store-count KPI drop from 353 to 273 looks inconsistent. Because the business is barely profitable, we grade valuation on EV/sales and EV/EBITDA rather than P/E. At 8.4× price/sales and 72× EV/EBITDA (P96 vs the broad market), with a 55.7× forward P/E and ROE of -0.8%, the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is that consensus EPS estimates are being cut (-5.8% in 30 days) while 7 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, plus integration risk from the new Utkarsh Classes acquisition. Together these set up a classic derating if margins don't recover.

Travel Food Services runs airport food courts, lounges and travel retail across 22 Indian airports, which gives it concession-based, semi-captive demand and a clear lead in its niche. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹878 cr (+20.1% YoY) and PAT was ₹276 cr (+43.1% YoY), so PAT margin rose to 31.4% from 26.4%. The implied Q2 (H1 less Q1) is about ₹426 cr revenue and ₹147 cr PAT. Revenue growth is steady at around +20% (Q1 FY27 was +20.6%) while margins are widening, and cash conversion is strong: CFO/PAT is 1.57x and net cash is ₹451 cr. The FY26 and Q3 FY26 rows in the trend table look misextracted (₹41 cr revenue, 1.4% margin) and I ignored them. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a lease-heavy concession operator. At 23.3x EV/EBITDA and 34.8x trailing P/E, it sits right at the broad-market median (P50/P49) and well below the 60–100x the sector card cites for Consumer Discretionary, with forward P/E (29.5x) below trailing and FY EPS estimates raised about 10% in 30 days, so it is fair, not cheap. P/B of 11.4x (P86) is rich, the stock is mid-way in its 52-week range, and the 80% dividend yield and 16.7 debt/equity in the snapshot are clearly data errors given the company says it has no traditional debt. The biggest risk is the Delhi Terminal 3 subsidiary (60% owned, material), whose licence expired on 30 Sept 2026. Losing or repricing that concession could take a meaningful chunk out of consolidated earnings, and management also says passenger traffic is softening.

fundamental.thesis: Vardhman Textiles is one of India's largest integrated textile makers, selling yarn, fabric and acrylic fibre. It is a cyclical, commodity-linked business and does not belong with the premium consumer franchises in its yfinance sector tag. Growth has picked up sharply: revenue growth rose from about +1% in FY26 to +13.3% in Q1 FY27 and about +15.6% in Q2 FY27. Q2 FY27 is derived as H1 minus Q1: revenue ₹2,866 cr and PAT ₹358 cr. Q2 PAT nearly doubled from ₹187 cr a year ago, and EBITDA margin jumped from 13.4% in FY26 to 21.5% in H1, with strong cash backing (CFO/PAT 1.48x, FCF ₹468 cr). Because the business is capital-intensive, valuation was graded on EV/EBITDA: at 15.2x it sits 35% below the market median, trailing P/E is 25.3x and forward P/E is 14.6x. That is offset by P/B of 1.85x on a weak 7.3% ROE and a price at 98% of its 52-week range, so the stock is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the margin jump is a cyclical peak driven by raw-material spreads rather than a lasting shift; next-year EPS estimates are already being trimmed (-2.5% over 30 days) and the sell-side mix leans hold/sell.

Technically the stock is a recovery attempt sitting just below a falling 200-day average (resistance near ₹24.35), not a confirmed breakout. fundamental.thesis: Trident is a Punjab-based home-textile and yarn maker that also runs a paper and chemicals business. In H1FY27 yarn is about 56% of revenue, towels about 35% and paper about 17%. H1FY27 revenue was flat at ₹3,506 cr (+0.3% YoY), but consolidated PAT jumped 44.5% to ₹334 cr on wider margins (EBITDA margin 18.6%, PAT margin 9.5%), with yarn EBIT nearly tripling to ₹337 cr. The implied Q2 is weaker on the top line: revenue of about ₹1,719 cr fell roughly 4% YoY after Q1's +4.7%, so revenue growth is decelerating even as PAT margin rose to about 10%. The table's 'accelerating' signal is unreliable because the older FY26 rows (₹171–670 cr) are clearly on a different basis. Because this is a capital-intensive manufacturer, I graded it mainly on EV/EBITDA: 15.7x is at P28 versus the broad market and below its median of 23.3x, and P/E of 35x trailing and 26x forward sits near the median. However, P/B of 2.8x against an ROE of only 8% is not cheap, so overall it is fair. The biggest risk is that the profit surge rests on one segment (yarn) while towels deteriorate (revenue -11%, EBIT -47%), just as the company commits to a ₹4,650 cr expansion worth about a third of its market cap.

technical.setup: Relief bounce inside a long-term downtrend: price is back above the 20-day average with MACD turning up and buying volume picking up, but it is still under the 50-day (₹73.71) and well below a falling 200-day (₹87.06) in a death-cross setup, and it keeps lagging both the Nifty and its sector peers, so this looks like a counter-trend rally, not a confirmed reversal.

Sentiment is bearish and the chart shows only a short bounce inside a long downtrend, with the price still below the 50-day (₹73.71) and 200-day averages. With little cash available (about ₹30.6k), a midcap with serious legal and governance risk does not justify new money, so we stay out until either the legal overhang clears or the price holds above ₹73.71.

fundamental.thesis: Zee Entertainment is India's second-largest broadcast media group (~50 TV channels plus the ZEE5 OTT platform), structurally pressured by the secular migration to streaming and left exposed after the Jiostar/Sony merger collapsed; it now carries substantial governance and legal overhangs that suppress any re-rating. FY26 annual revenue declined 1.9% YoY to ₹7,567 Cr while PAT collapsed 82.8% to ₹120 Cr, compressing PAT margin to 1.6% and EBITDA margin to a catastrophic 2.6% (from 13.4% in FY25) — the multi-quarter trajectory shows revenue decelerating and margins contracting across every available period with no stabilisation evident in filings. Forward P/E of 13.42× (P19 vs broad-market peers, -42% below median) and P/B of 0.9× (P2 vs peers, -80% below median) both screen as unambiguously cheap; EV/EBITDA of 23× looks deceptively at median but is computed on severely depressed EBITDA — on normalised 12-13% margins the implied EV/EBITDA would be sub-5×, confirming franchise-level cheapness if operational recovery is achievable. The single largest risk to the recovery thesis is the IDBI Bank insolvency petition (filed September 2025) seeking NCLT-admitted CIRP initiation, which if granted would be existential for the business regardless of underlying brand and content-IP value.

drivers: Management kept guidance unchanged ('15% CAGR real growth commitment'), but flagged that Aluminum EBIT margin 'collapsed to 6.5% in Q2' (normal is 12-13%). Recovery depends on OEM price resets.

No company headlines in the last 7 days and Auto sector flows are neutral, so nothing offsets the post-results weakness. This is a midcap, so conviction is kept moderate.

fundamental.thesis: Craftsman Automation makes engine and powertrain parts, aluminium products (61% of H1 revenue) and industrial and engineering products, and German operations contributed 17% of H1 revenue, so some of the growth may be acquired rather than organic. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 47.0% YoY to Rs 2,945 cr and PAT rose 68% to Rs 153 cr, with revenue growth picking up from +30.5% in Q3 FY26 to +36.3% in Q1 FY27 (although below the +55% to +65% of H1 FY26), but EBITDA margin fell from 16.8% to 14.0% in one quarter and PAT rose only 1.3% QoQ despite about 21% more revenue. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 23.5x only matches the median of a broad-market peer set rather than close auto-parts peers, and it looks full next to a 60.98x trailing P/E (P79, above the 18-28x auto benchmark), a 32.98x forward P/E and 8.53x P/B, so the valuation is expensive. The main risk is that this price needs a margin recovery while FY-EPS estimates have been cut 6.2%, FY26 FCF was Rs -667 cr and two more plants are being built, and confidence is limited by data problems: Q3 FY26 revenue of Rs 206 cr looks wrong (its PAT and margin imply about Rs 2,058 cr), the price implied by the sell-side target conflicts with the 94.2% 52-week position, the 9.0% dividend yield looks unreliable, and debt/equity of 111.01 is probably 1.11x but unconfirmed.

Belrise Industries is a mid-cap auto-component maker focused on metal fabrication. It holds about 24% of the two-wheeler metal-fabrication market, supplies 38 OEMs from 27 plants in India, and 71% of its revenue comes from parts that work in both petrol and electric vehicles. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 14.7% YoY to ₹5,293 cr and adjusted PAT grew 17.7% to ₹288 cr, after Q1 FY27 growth of +12.6% revenue and +8.9% PAT, so profit growth picked up in Q2 (PAT +25%). But margins are slipping: EBITDA margin fell 70 bps from 12.5% to 11.8% and PAT margin is thin at 5.4%. The older rows in the trend table use mixed units and are unreliable, so the stated 'accelerating revenue' signal cannot be trusted. On valuation, the main yardstick for a capital-intensive ancillary is EV/EBITDA, which is 18.1x (22% below the broad-market median); trailing P/E of 41x is above the 18–28x auto range, while forward P/E of 25x is inside it, so overall the stock is fair. With the price at 96% of its 52-week range, near-term upside looks limited. The biggest risk is that sell-side EPS estimates were cut 8.6% over 90 days while all 6 analysts still rate it buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating if margins keep compressing.

The positives are offset by risks: the trading business fell 19% on Middle East disruptions, steel and polymer costs are still high and price hikes to customers may lag, and staff costs went up. The transcript is 86 days old, close to the 90-day staleness limit.

drivers: H1FY27 results: revenue up 20.8% YoY to Rs. 2,673.4 crore, but PBT up only 9.96%, so margins are shrinking; management gave no forward guidance

fundamental.thesis: E.I.D. Parry is a holding company. The 10.1x forward P/E rests on a forecast earnings rebound, yet analysts have cut forward estimates about 30% over 90 days, so that forward number is unreliable.

Using EV/EBITDA, because this is a low-margin, commodity-heavy business, the stock trades at 25.0x, slightly above the market median of 23.3x (P55). Its trailing P/E of 25.4x looks cheap against the 40-60x FMCG range, but that discount reflects the edible-oil mix rather than mispricing, so the grade is fair even though the price sits near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that edible-oil margins keep shrinking, and if receivables keep rising (up about ₹1,139 cr in H1) while net debt stays at ₹2,198 cr, strong sales growth may not translate into profit or cash.

fundamental.thesis: Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

On the sector card's yardstick (pre-sales momentum, collections, net debt), with P/E set aside, I grade valuation fair, not cheap: the 10.2x trailing P/E looks cheap against peers but is meaningless here, P/B of 5.8x sits above the broad-market median, and next-year EPS estimates were cut about 33% in 30 days, which leaves the stock near its 52-week low (12% of range) for a reason. The biggest risk is that falling bookings and collections are an early sign of NCR demand fatigue at peak prices, while the company is buying more land (Farrukhnagar, Sohna, DXP).

ITI is a loss-making, state-owned maker of telecom and defence-communications equipment that depends on a government revival plan. It is not a telecom operator, so the sector card's ARPU and tariff priors do not apply. In the latest extracted quarter (Q1 FY27), revenue fell 14.6% YoY to ₹425 cr from ₹498 cr, a sharper drop than the -4.2% in Q1 FY26. The net loss narrowed to ₹32.25 cr from ₹63.61 cr, so PAT margin improved from about -12.8% to about -7.6%, but the company still loses money at the operating level (EBITDA margin only 1-4%). Q2 FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-13 but are not yet extracted, so these figures may be stale. Because the business is capital-intensive and has thin or negative earnings, EV/EBITDA is the yardstick: at 483× it is far above the 9-12× telecom norm and the 28-45× P/E range for capital goods, and P/B of 13.3× (P90 vs the broad market) on a loss-making book is clearly expensive. The trailing P/E of 79× is unreliable because it is likely boosted by the ₹449 cr one-off exceptional gain in FY26. The order-book and revival-funding figures in the extract look like unit errors (lakh vs crore), so they have not been relied on, and the stock sitting near its 52-week low does not make up for the weak fundamentals.

drivers: Auditors gave a 'disclaimer of opinion' on Q1FY27 results, citing revenue-recognition gaps under Ind AS 115, inventory obsolescence and weak internal controls. This is a governance red flag and outweighs the positives.

Results are still weak: revenue fell 14.6% YoY to Rs. 425.03 crore and the consolidated loss was Rs. 32.25 crore. Management gave no forward guidance, only milestone notes on unbilled revenue and the ASCON Phase IV proof of concept.

The positives are the Ministry of Defence order book (ASCON Phase IV, Rs. 8,280.36 crore) and continued Government of India revival support. The headline order-book figure of 'Rs. 13,88,281 crore' looks like a unit error (probably lakh, not crore), so don't rely on it.

There is little else to go on: management tone is 94 days old, there is no earnings-surprise data, no headlines in the last 7 days, and sector flow is neutral. Conviction is kept low for a midcap with this little evidence.

fundamental.thesis: Prime Focus (PFOCUS) is a media-services company that is unprofitable or only marginally profitable on a trailing basis. fundamental.thesis: DLF is NCR's leading luxury housing developer, and it also earns rental income through its DCCDL office and retail arm, which brings in about ₹6,800 cr a year. Because property sales are booked as revenue only on completion, I judged it on operating numbers rather than P&L: Q2FY27 pre-sales were ₹3,800 cr, below the FY26 run-rate of about ₹5,000 cr a quarter (₹20,143 cr for the year), while reported revenue was ₹2,298 cr and PAT ₹1,301 cr (+11% YoY, 56.6% margin, lifted by the JV share and other income). The 'expanding margin' signal mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so I don't treat it as a real trend; the stronger evidence is cash from operations at 1.43x PAT and a net cash balance of ₹9,300–15,000 cr (the filings disagree) even after a ₹1,980 cr dividend. For valuation I used the sector yardstick (pre-sales, net cash and the rental annuity) instead of P/E or EV/EBITDA, since both are distorted by the revenue lag; at a ₹1.4L cr market cap, P/B of 3.2x with 10% ROE, and the stock at 23.5% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair. The main risk is that this quarter's soft bookings continue if the Mumbai, Magnolias 2 and Hamilton launches slip, as analysts have already cut FY EPS estimates by 4.8% over 90 days while 20 of 22 still rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Vedanta is a diversified natural-resources producer (aluminium, zinc, oil & gas, iron ore, power) that sells at global commodity prices, so it is judged on its cost position and balance sheet. Its continuing operations shrank after the demerger: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹59,872 cr, down 22.9% YoY, and Q2 revenue fell to ₹26,356 cr from ₹33,515 cr in Q1. Profit is improving even though sales are shrinking: H1 PAT rose 83% YoY to ₹9,123 cr, but Q2 PAT of ₹3,650 cr was below Q1's ₹5,473 cr, with PAT margin slipping from 16.4% to 13.8%. Prior periods were restated for the demerger, so the YoY comparisons are not clean. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, as the sector card advises for commodity names, the stock is cheap: 5.71x is the lowest of 16 Materials peers (sector median 17.9x) and at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle band. Forward P/E of 12.7x vs trailing 17.75x, and analysts raising FY EPS estimates by 25% over 90 days, point the same way. The main risks are that Q2 revenue and profit both fell from Q1, and that several data points don't reconcile (yfinance Q2 revenue ₹11,229 cr vs ₹26,356 cr in the filing, a 1038% dividend yield, and a 52-week range distorted by the demerger), so the inputs carry real uncertainty.
