fundamental.thesis: Godrej Consumer Products is India's largest home and personal care company, commanding leadership in household insecticides (Goodknight), hair colour (Godrej Expert), and liquid detergents, with material EM exposure across Africa, Indonesia, and Latin America that amplifies both growth and FX risk. Q4FY26 (latest official quarter) showed revenue of ₹3,885 cr (+11.0% YoY, recovering sharply from +4.0% in Q2FY26) with PAT of ₹452 cr (+10.0% YoY), and volume growth accelerating to 8% from 3% two quarters prior — a genuine demand signal — though full-year FY26 PAT was up just +0.5% on +8.5% revenue growth, reflecting margin headwinds that only partially normalised by year-end. At trailing P/E of 54.9× the stock sits within the 40–65× FMCG sector card range but at P80 vs household-and-personal-care peers (+25% premium to sector median), making it expensive on peer-relative terms; however, forward P/E of 36.3× (vs trailing) signals meaningful earnings recovery is priced in, and the stock trading near its 52-week low (7.8% of range) provides modestly better entry optics than the headline multiple suggests. The biggest risk is the combination of elevated reported debt/equity (34.9) with active Argentina-hyperinflation drag (₹13.5 cr profit headwind cited in Q1FY27 exceptional items) and consistent downward EPS estimate revisions (-1.6% over 90 days), which could cap re-rating even if the domestic volume recovery continues.

fundamental.thesis: UCO Bank is a mid-sized, government-owned lender with gross advances of ₹2,87,690 cr. Its loan book is growing faster each quarter (+16.6% YoY in Q2FY26, +21.2% in Q1FY27, +24.7% in Q2FY27). Q2FY27 net profit rose 26.8% YoY to ₹786 cr, up from +8.1% growth in Q1FY27, and asset quality kept improving: gross NPA fell from 2.56% to 1.96% and net NPA from 0.43% to 0.18% over four quarters, with provision coverage at 98.4%. Net interest income (NII) of ₹2,886 cr is about 13.9% above the year-ago revenue line of ₹2,533 cr, but that row may not be strictly NII, so treat the growth figure as approximate. For a bank we judge value on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE), not P/E. P/B of 1.05x is cheap against the market and peers, but ROE is only 8.6% and return on assets 0.8%, well below the 12% ROE needed to call it cheap, so we grade it fair; the 12.7x trailing P/E against a 20.0x forward P/E also suggests the market expects earnings to fall. The biggest risk is funding: loans are growing about 25% while CASA (current and savings account) deposits grow only 10.6%. As a result, the CASA ratio slid from 38.65% to 36.77% and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%. That pressures margins as the bank pays more for deposits, and it comes in a risk-off market where foreign investors are selling financials.

fundamental.thesis: Engineers India is a state-owned engineering consultancy and turnkey contractor for hydrocarbon, refinery and petrochemical projects, so its revenue comes from working through its order book. H1FY27 revenue fell 8.2% YoY to ₹1,644 cr, and the implied Q2 figure (about ₹824 cr, H1 minus Q1) is down roughly 10% YoY, after +36% to +45% growth in FY26. That makes revenue a clear deceleration story: Turnkey revenue collapsed 46.7%, while the higher-margin Consultancy segment grew 32.9%. That mix shift lifted H1 PAT 138% to ₹355 cr, PAT margin from 8.3% to 21.6% and EBITDA margin to 28.4%. Cash conversion was strong at 1.76x CFO/PAT. Using EV/EBITDA, the Industrials sector card's preferred measure for order-book businesses, the stock trades at 16.75x against a market median of 23.3x (P30), and trailing P/E is 20.6x against the 28–45x Industrials range, so it looks cheap. But it sits at 87% of its 52-week range, and next-FY earnings estimates were cut 8.1% over 90 days, which tempers the upside. Revenue growth accelerated from +23.0% in Q1FY27 to +38.5% in Q2FY27 (Rs 3,777 cr, with domestic wires and cables up 45.76%), and management raised FY27 growth guidance to 25%+ from 20%, but profit lagged: PAT rose only +29.0% to Rs 262 cr, down from Rs 274 cr in Q1, while PAT margin fell from 8.6% to 7.0% and EBITDA margin from 13.0% to 10.6%, below the roughly 11% guided for FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock looks expensive at 40.9x (P83 and 75% above the broad-market median, as no tight peer set is available), with trailing P/E of 58.7x above the 28-45x sector range and the price at 97.5% of its 52-week range; the listed +25% consensus upside looks wrong, because the Rs 53,828 cr market cap implies a price near Rs 5,630, which is above the Rs 5,098 mean target. The biggest risk is that a stock priced for perfection de-rates if margins stay under pressure while growth is chased and Sanand capex of about Rs 600 cr a year continues, with FY-EPS estimates already cut 2.5% over the last 30 days; the snapshot's 3.8 debt/equity and 8.0% dividend yield look like data-scale errors and were not relied on.

3M India is the listed Indian arm of 3M, selling diversified products across four segments: Safety & Industrial, Transportation & Electronics, Healthcare and Consumer. It sells catalogue products rather than working through an order book, so the sector card's order-book yardstick does not fit, and I graded it on EV/EBITDA and P/E. In the latest quarter we have extracted figures for (Q1 FY27), revenue grew 19.0% to ₹1,423 cr and PAT grew 31.1% to ₹233 cr (16.4% PAT margin). Revenue growth has picked up from +12.7% in Q3 FY26 and has been double-digit for 5 quarters in a row, led by Healthcare (+23.5%) and Safety & Industrial (+23.0%). Two caveats: EBITDA margin slipped to 17.6% from about 20% in FY26, and the Q3 FY26 loss of ₹62 cr looks like a one-off item, not a fall in the core business. Q2 FY27 results were filed on 6 Nov but are missing from the trend table. Valuation is expensive on our yardstick: trailing P/E is 64.1x against an Industrials range of 28-45x, EV/EBITDA is 36.5x against a market median of 23.3x (77th percentile), and P/B is 20.9x (96th percentile). The forward P/E of 42.2x shows strong earnings growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is that analysts cut FY earnings estimates by 6.5% in the last 30 days, right after the Q2 results we have not seen, which suggests a weak quarter at a premium multiple. That is a classic setup for the stock to re-rate lower.

fundamental.thesis: ICICI Bank is India's second-largest private-sector bank, with a large retail and business-banking franchise and subsidiaries in life and general insurance. In Q2FY27, consolidated revenue rose 15.8% YoY to ₹88,161cr, up from +6.9% growth in Q1. PAT rose 21.5% YoY to ₹17,389cr, up from +12.6%, but PAT margin slipped from 20.4% to 19.7%. Net interest margin (NIM) has also fallen from 4.36% to 4.18% in one quarter, and the share of low-cost CASA deposits dropped from 38.1% to 35.8%; on the positive side, gross NPA improved to 1.2% and net NPA to 0.30%, with provision coverage at 75%. Following the sector card, I value lenders on price-to-book against ROE: P/B of 2.48x with a 16.4% ROE is fair for a top-quality bank, even though it ranks P93 (expensive) on P/B among its 15 bank peers, and the stock sits at 22% of its 52-week range, which makes for a reasonable entry point. The biggest risk is that management expects two more 25bp repo hikes and says NIM will only bottom after Q3, so margins could compress further before they recover.

H1FY27 revenue was ₹97,454 cr, up only +1.9% YoY (Q2 constant-currency growth +1.5%, down from +2.4% in Q1 and +3.1% for FY26). H1 PAT was ₹15,613 cr, up +9.2%, but PAT margin slipped from 16.5% to 16.0%, and the FY27 revenue guide was cut to 1–2% cc from 1.5–3.5% even though the trend table labels it 'maintained'. Using trailing P/E as the yardstick for an asset-light IT services firm, 15.8× sits well below the 22–30× sector range and 36% below the peer median of 24.7× (P12), so the stock grades cheap, at about 10–18% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that the discount is a value trap: shrinking legacy revenue, a guidance cut and small but steady estimate cuts (-0.3% over 30 days) may mean the low multiple reflects a lasting slowdown rather than a mispricing.

fundamental.thesis: Sun Pharma is India's largest drugmaker. It earns from India branded formulations (market share up 0.3pp to 8.6%, formulations growth +16.6%), emerging markets (+16.7%), global innovative medicines (21.5% of sales, +9.8%) and a shrinking US generics book. Revenue is steady rather than accelerating. H1FY27 revenue was ₹31,499 cr (+11.0% YoY), with Q1 at +10.1% and an implied Q2 of about ₹16,315 cr (+11.8%), down from +15.1% in the 9MFY26 window. Reported PAT fell 9.5% to ₹4,883 cr, and the implied Q2 PAT margin is only about 12.2%, hit by Organon deal costs and the US pricing-settlement charge. US formulations fell 8.2% in Q2 as Lenalidomide sales eroded. EBITDA margin held at about 29%. I graded valuation on trailing P/E against the Healthcare band of 28-40x because Sun is a non-capital-intensive pharma name. At 37.4x it sits inside the band and at P54 among 13 pharma peers, so it is fair rather than cheap. EV/EBITDA of 24.2x is a 13% premium to the peer median, though forward P/E of 27.7x does price in earnings recovery. The biggest risk is the USD 14bn Organon acquisition, which is far larger than the roughly ₹17,700 cr of net cash. It brings integration costs and balance-sheet strain, more costs are still to come, and sell-side EPS estimates are being cut (-2.9% over 30 days, -3.4% over 90 days) even though 29 of 34 analysts rate it a buy.

The most usable figures are for H1 FY27: revenue rose about 31% YoY to roughly ₹1,00,575 cr, but PAT fell 18.3% to about ₹5,767 cr and PAT margin was 5.7% (vs 8.3% in the FY26 row), so volume growth is not turning into profit growth. The 1H FY26, FY26 and 9MFY26 rows plus the motorcycle/marine KPIs look like parent Suzuki Motor Corporation data mixed in, and Q2 FY27 standalone numbers are missing, so the trend is unreliable. On the auto-OEM yardstick (P/E plus EV/EBITDA vs peers), the stock trades at 27.6x trailing P/E (inside the 18–30x OEM band, P60 vs peers), 20.8x forward P/E and 18.3x EV/EBITDA (exactly at the peer median), so it is fairly valued. It sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, but falling profits and sharply negative analyst estimate revisions argue against treating that as a value entry.

fundamental.thesis: ONGC is India's largest upstream oil and gas producer, a state-run company whose earnings rise with crude prices, and that upside is limited by government policy such as windfall taxes. The indexed trend table is stale and only runs to FY26, when revenue fell 3.9% to ₹132,508 cr and PAT fell 7.6% to ₹32,894 cr, continuing a steady decline. The 5 Nov filing headline points to a sharp turnaround: Q2 FY27 standalone PAT of ₹15,489 cr, roughly +57% versus an implied ₹9,848 cr in Q2 FY26, and a record H1 PAT of ₹32,522 cr (+82% YoY). FY EPS estimates were raised 5.4% over the last 30 days. On the yardstick the sector card names for PSU upstream (P/E plus dividend yield, EV/EBITDA), the stock trades at 8.0x trailing P/E, inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, at 4.6x EV/EBITDA (25% below the peer median of 6.1x) and at 0.9x book with 12.7% ROE, so I grade it fair (policy-priced) rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the rebound comes from elevated crude caused by the West Asia conflict, not from higher volumes, so a crude pullback or a new windfall levy could reverse it quickly.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Enterprises is the Adani group's incubator. It runs airports, roads, data centres (through the AdaniConneX JV), mining services and new energy manufacturing, and it is still building most of these businesses with heavy capital spending. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹70,140 cr, up 62.3% YoY, and the jump seems to come from new capacity coming on stream. Profit has not kept up. H1 PAT was a ₹241 cr loss (-0.3% margin) against a ₹9,951 cr FY26 profit at a 9.9% margin. EBITDA margin fell from 25.6% in FY26 to 15.0%. Working back from the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 alone made about ₹919 cr PAT on about ₹36,594 cr revenue (about 2.5% margin). The yfinance peer set is oil and gas companies, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA as the Industrials card suggests. At 36.5x EV/EBITDA, 41.1x trailing P/E and 4.8x P/B with only 13.7% ROE, the stock is expensive. The forward P/E of 53.6x is above the trailing P/E, and next-year EPS estimates were cut 14.6% in the last 30 days. The price is at 98.5% of its 52-week range, so very little bad news is priced in. The biggest risk is cash burn: H1 free cash flow was -₹10,800 cr and FY26 was -₹31,012 cr, and the company has needed a QIP and a rights issue to fund this, so any delay in turning new capacity into profit means more dilution or more debt.

Bajaj Finserv is a holding company whose value comes mostly from its controlling stake in Bajaj Finance (AUM ₹5.84L cr, up 26%, gross NPA 1.06%), plus Bajaj Housing Finance and its life and general insurance businesses. In Q2FY27, consolidated revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹43,416 cr, slowing from +19.2% in Q1FY27, while PAT grew faster, rising 25.0% to ₹5,952 cr (from +18.1%), for a 13.7% PAT margin. The big margin jump from the FY26 and Q3FY26 rows (5.6–6.5%) probably reflects a mix of consolidated and attributable figures rather than a real 2x improvement, so I do not count it as margin expansion. Life insurance did well (VNB up 40%, new-business margin up to 21.6%), but general insurance was weak (PAT down 19%, combined ratio 104.5%). Following the sector card, I valued it on P/B against ROE, as for a lender or holding company, not on P/E. At 3.53x book with a 14.6% ROE it ranks P73 among peers on both P/B and trailing P/E (28.2x vs a 17.5x median), with forward P/E at 18.7x. That is a full price for a holding company that usually trades at a discount to its parts, offset partly by the stock sitting at only 21% of its 52-week range, so my verdict is fair, not cheap. The biggest risk to the thesis is that analysts are cutting earnings estimates (next-FY estimates down 3.0% over 90 days) even though 11 of 13 rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating. Other risks are elevated general-insurance claims and a slowdown in revenue growth.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Steel is one of India's largest integrated steelmakers, and its profits come mostly from the high-margin India business, which posted an EBITDA margin of about 25% in Q2FY27; the loss-making European plants in the Netherlands (TSN) and the UK (TSUK) pull the group numbers down. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹65,436 cr, up 11.5% YoY, and PAT was ₹3,700 cr, up 16.3% YoY, for a PAT margin of 5.7%. The pre-computed signal calls revenue growth 'accelerating', but it actually slowed from +14.3% in Q1. Group EBITDA margin improved from 15.4% to 16.3% and EBITDA per tonne rose from ₹12,898 to ₹13,462, but the India EBITDA margin slipped from 26.8% to 25.0%. Part of the reported PAT may be the ₹3,457 cr one-off accounting gain from the TMILL stake revaluation (Aug 2026), so the underlying profit quality is unclear. Management expects a stronger H2: India realisations up ₹3,500–3,600/t in Q3, ₹7,000 cr of cost savings targeted for FY27 (₹1,800 cr delivered so far), and a UK breakeven in Q4. Analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% and next-FY estimates by about 9%. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-intensive steelmaker. At 10.4× it sits at P13 among Materials peers, but that peer group is skewed by paint companies and looks rich against the 5–8× mid-cycle range for steel. The forward P/E of 10.8× against a trailing 23.5× already prices in strong earnings growth, and other steel names (JSWSTEEL, JINDALSTEL, HINDALCO) are cheaper, so I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is the Netherlands unit: regulators may revoke key plant permits, it is flagged as a going concern with material uncertainty, there is a large unrecognised impairment risk, and the auditor has issued a modified opinion. Net debt of ₹91,423 cr (2.4× EBITDA) adds to that risk.

fundamental.thesis: SBI Card is India's #2 credit-card issuer, a mono-line lender with about 18.5% share of cards and 18.2% of spends, earning on revolver interest and fees. On the lender yardstick (price-to-book against ROE, not P/E), 3.6x book against a 14.7% trailing ROE (18.4% in the latest quarter) is fair to slightly rich: it ranks P78 on P/B and P67 on trailing P/E among credit-services peers, though the stock sits near its 52-week low, the 16.3x forward P/E is below the 26x trailing, and FY EPS estimates were raised about 7% over 30 days. The main risk is that profit growth is coming from credit-cost relief while the loan book shrinks, and that lever runs out once asset quality normalises.

Mphasis is a mid-sized Indian IT services company with a heavy tilt toward banking and insurance clients. Almost all its revenue (98.6%) comes from direct clients, and it is repositioning around AI-led work through Mphasis.AI and its Tria platform. Growth has picked up: constant-currency revenue growth rose from +7.1% YoY in Q4FY26 to +11.3% in Q2FY27, and PAT grew +19.0% YoY. Management raised its FY27 revenue guidance from high single digits to low double digits, and the deal pipeline hit a record $9.3 Bn, up 23% YoY. That is well ahead of the sector, where tier-1 names are growing near zero. However, operating margin is flat at 14.8%, down from 15.3% a year ago, and cash conversion is weak: FY26 operating cash flow was only 0.67x PAT, and receivable days (DSO) jumped to 113 from 95. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA for this asset-light IT business. Trailing P/E of 24.7x sits inside the 22–30x IT sector range and exactly at the peer median (P50). EV/EBITDA is also at the median (14.7x), and P/B of 4.4x is at P25. Forward P/E of 18.3x is below trailing, which means earnings growth is expected, and the stock sits at 30% of its 52-week range. Overall that grades as fair, with a mildly favourable entry point. The biggest risk is that AI-led deals turn out to cannibalise legacy revenue rather than add to it, which would compress margins while the slow cash collection continues.

Q2FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹9,300 cr (+23.8% YoY from ₹7,512 cr), PAT surged 118.9% to ₹821 cr (margin 8.8%), confirming a clear multi-period turnaround: PAT margins have expanded from -0.7% in H1FY26 through 4.5%, 4.7%, 4.9%, to 8.8% now, with H1FY27 PAT of ₹1,198 cr vs a ₹80.6 cr loss a year ago. The fertiliser business is subsidy-driven and does not match the sector card's steel/cement/paints yardsticks, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 17.3x it is close to the peer median of 17.9x (P47). Trailing P/E is 31.6x, below the peer median of 37.3x but above the 12–22x Materials benchmark, so overall it is fair, not cheap. P&G Hygiene & Health Care is a debt-free, standalone FMCG company with leading feminine-hygiene (Whisper) and healthcare (Vicks) brands, a 114.9% ROE and strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.16x in H1FY27). fundamental.thesis: Petronet LNG runs India's largest LNG import and regasification terminals (Dahej, now expanded to 22.5 MTPA, plus Kochi). It earns mainly on volumes and regas tariffs, so LNG price swings flow through revenue without much effect on profit. fundamental.thesis: Indian Energy Exchange runs India's dominant power exchange, an asset-light trading platform where most revenue (77-78%) comes from transaction fees. Real-Time Market volumes have grown from 20% of its electricity volumes in FY23 to 41% in H1 FY27. In Q2FY27 revenue rose +10.8% YoY to ₹203 cr and PAT rose +12.9% to ₹139 cr, a 68.5% PAT margin. Revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q1FY26 and +14.6% for FY26 to roughly 10-11% over the last three periods, though margins are steady to rising. Cash conversion is only moderate, with CFO/PAT of 0.73x in H1FY27 versus 0.88x in FY26. Because this is a fee-based exchange rather than a lender, I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA, not the bank P/B yardstick. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.3x is 37% below the broad-market median of 35.2x, EV/EBITDA of 14.2x is at P24, ROE is 39%, and the stock sits at about 9% of its 52-week range. Part of that discount is fair given the regulatory overhang, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 5.5% over 90 days, so the stock is not mispriced beyond doubt.

IFCI is a government-owned development finance institution. Most of its legacy lending book is still impaired, and much of its reported income comes from subsidiaries (such as its stock-broking and infrastructure arms) and treasury and recovery gains rather than from a healthy, growing loan book. The extracted filings show FY26 revenue of about ₹2,069 cr (+2.5% YoY) and PAT of ₹181 cr (+5.7%). Growth has slowed from +13.4% in H1FY26 to roughly flat, and PAT margin has narrowed from 13.6% in H1FY26 to 8.7% for the full year. The H1 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-12 show only credit-quality figures, with no revenue or PAT extracted yet, and the yfinance Q2FY27 row (₹604 cr revenue, ₹149 cr PAT) is unverified for a financial company. Credit quality is extremely weak and getting worse: gross NPA is 99.23% and net NPA 95.55% in H1 FY27, up from 95.79% and 78.44% in FY26, and the capital adequacy ratio (CRAR) is negative at -18.42%. For a lender, the right test is price-to-book against return on equity, and the stock fails it. P/B is 2.43x for a business earning about 0.7% ROA (FY26) with negative regulatory capital, so 'expensive' is the right grade, and the 119x trailing P/E (P96 against the broad market) confirms it. A P/B of 2.4x looks cheap only next to the broad-market median. The 23x forward P/E assumes a large earnings jump that the filings do not yet support. The biggest risk is that the price depends on government recapitalisation or restructuring hopes rather than on the core business. A disappointing H1 FY27 print, or any delay in capital support, could cut the valuation sharply. This is a midcap with thin disclosure, so conviction stays moderate.

fundamental.thesis: SBFC Finance is a mid-sized, profitable NBFC lender classed by RBI as Middle Layer, with gross loans of Rs 11,161 cr and ROA of about 4.6%. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 33.0% YoY to Rs 547 cr, up from an implied +26.5% in Q1 (the pre-computed 'decelerating' signal mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods), but PAT growth slowed to +27.2% at Rs 139 cr from +34.0% in Q3 FY26, PAT margin slipped from 27.7% to 25.4% over the same three quarters, and AUM growth eased from 30.7% at FY26 to 27.0%. fundamental.thesis: NBCC (India) is a Navratna PSU operating primarily as a Project Management Consultant (PMC) on government construction projects, with smaller EPC and real estate segments — a near-debt-free government-backed execution engine whose revenue visibility depends almost entirely on public-sector order flow. Schneider Electric Infrastructure is a midcap maker of medium-voltage switchgear and electrical distribution equipment. It is positioned in India's power-transmission, data-centre, semiconductor-fab and renewables build-out, with record Q2 FY27 orders of ₹1,265 cr (+50.9% YoY) and an order backlog of ₹2,701 cr (+49.6% YoY). EBITDA margin fell from 13.6% to 8.4%, and H1 PAT was down 55%, because the company could not pass on copper, aluminium and steel costs fast enough and finance costs rose about 39%. We grade valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive industrials. At 76.6× (P96 vs the broad market, versus a median of 23.3×), a 146.8× trailing P/E, 55.3× forward P/E and a price at 86% of its 52-week range, the stock is clearly expensive. The biggest risk is that margins stay weak while analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (FY EPS -30% over 30 days, -44% over 90 days). The pre-acquisition business is mixed: consumables revenue grew about 30% YoY with EBITDA margin up to 22.4%, and the ex-Molycop order book grew 21%, but the equipment segment shrank and management cut FY27 equipment growth guidance from 25% to 15%. The biggest risk is the debt taken on to fund the deal: borrowings rose from about ₹318 cr to about ₹11,492 cr while Molycop is still loss-making. Integration, and how much cash the combined business can generate, now decide the equity story more than the base business does.

The biggest risk is that the hoped-for H2 festive and wedding recovery fails to arrive while losses keep growing, which would keep the business dependent on external funding (the planned $100-150M TMRW raise and separate debt raises at the ethnic subsidiaries).

The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

Using the OEM P/E band from the sector card (18-30x) as the yardstick, the stock looks expensive at 36.2x trailing earnings with EV/EBITDA of 21.2x; the 23.8x forward P/E is within the band, but it relies on a margin recovery while current-year EPS estimates have been cut 13.8% in 30 days. The biggest risk is that volume growth keeps failing to reach profit if commodity costs stay high, which would leave the expected earnings rebound and the bullish 26-of-29 analyst buy ratings exposed.

Olectra Greentech is a mid-cap maker of electric buses (Mobility Division, about 86% of revenue) and composite insulators (Energy Division, about 14%), and it sells heavily to state transport bodies through its STU partnerships. Taking H1FY27 minus Q1FY27, Q2FY27 revenue was about ₹687 cr, up only about 4.5% from about ₹657 cr a year earlier, a sharp slowdown from +65.7% in Q1FY27 and +28.8% in Q3FY26. Q2 PAT was about ₹52 cr (+4% YoY), and EBITDA margin has fallen steadily from 16.1% to 10.4% over the trend window, so the table's 'accelerating' label hides a slowing quarter. Using P/E against the Auto OEM norm (the reported EV/EBITDA of 1,066× is clearly a data error), the trailing P/E of 56× is far above the sector card's 18–30× OEM band and sits at P75 vs the broad market, with P/B of 8.1× at P73, so the stock is expensive even after allowing for the forward P/E of 27.9×. Cash generation did improve, with H1FY27 operating cash flow at 2.42× PAT and positive free cash flow of ₹146 cr. The biggest risk is that growth stalls at a high multiple while margins keep falling and finance costs stay high.

Inventurus Knowledge Solutions (IKS) runs outsourced back-office, revenue-cycle and clinical-documentation services for more than 1,900 US healthcare organisations, and over 90% of its revenue comes from repeat clients. Q2FY27 revenue roughly doubled, up 103.9% YoY to ₹1,592 cr, but most of that comes from buying TruBridge (only 82 days of it are included), not from the legacy business, which management says is growing 13-14%. Before the deal, growth was steady at about +20% (Q1FY27 +20.7%, FY26 +19.9%). PAT rose only 20.4% to ₹218 cr, so the PAT margin fell from 23.1% to 13.7%, the EBITDA margin fell from 34.8% to 27.7%, and finance costs rose 531% on acquisition debt. This is a tech-enabled healthcare services business rather than classic IT services, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus forward P/E. EV/EBITDA of 25.4x is in line with the broad-market median (P57). Trailing P/E of 39.8x is above the 22-30x IT range but within the 28-40x healthcare range, and forward P/E of 25.7x prices in a recovery. Overall that is fair, not cheap, and the 10.4x P/B is rich at P83. The biggest risk is that the TruBridge integration does not bring margins back to the early-to-mid-30s target. Sell-side earnings estimates are already being cut (FY EPS -5.1% over 30 days, -6.5% over 90 days) while 8 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a stock is re-rated lower.

fundamental.thesis: Latent View Analytics is a mid-cap data-analytics and AI consulting firm with about 1,800 employees and 40 Fortune 500 clients; it is still growing much faster than tier-1 Indian IT, which is close to flat. Growth is slowing quarter by quarter, though. Revenue growth fell from +27.3% YoY in H1FY26 and +24.3% in FY26 to +14.2% in Q2FY27 (₹294 cr). Q2 PAT was ₹48 cr (+6.1% YoY), and H1FY27 PAT was flat at -0.8% even though revenue grew 17.7%. Margins are shrinking because employee costs rose 21.8% YoY and now take 68.8% of revenue, and outside Industrials (+21.4%) the segments are barely growing (Financial Services +3.5%, CPG/Retail +2.7%). Trailing P/E of 23.65× sits within the IT sector benchmark range of 22–30×, grading FAIR; however, forward P/E of 17.21× falls significantly below the sector lower bound and the EV/EBITDA of 15.15× is at a 35% discount to the broad-market median (23.3×), and with the stock at just 7.4% of its 52-week range (near lows), risk/reward tilts incrementally toward cheap — primary yardstick used is P/E + EV/EBITDA given the IT services capital-light model. The biggest risk is that a 73.9% US revenue concentration faces the active RISK_OFF macro headwind (IT sector macro underweight, rising US yields), while an anomalously high D/E of 9.58× — atypical for an IT peer and possibly inflated by Ind AS 116 leases plus the pending €160M Randstad acquisition — adds balance-sheet uncertainty that is not yet resolved.

fundamental.thesis: NLC India is a state-owned lignite miner and power generator. It earns mostly regulated returns on thermal capacity, and it is growing its renewables business, where generation rose 31.9% in H1FY27. Revenue growth is solid: H1FY27 revenue was Rs 9,449 cr (+18.1% YoY). Working back from H1 and Q1, Q2FY27 revenue was about Rs 4,732 cr (+13.3% YoY), slower than Q1's +23.2%. Profit is much less steady. Q1FY27 PAT fell 46% to Rs 429 cr (9.1% margin), while implied Q2 PAT was about Rs 1,335 cr (roughly +114% YoY, 28% margin), which may include one-off regulatory items. The EBITDA margin trend is down, from 37–38% to about 30.5% for FY26. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA and P/B plus ROE, as the sector card suggests for capital-intensive regulated utilities. EV/EBITDA is 9.9x, P/B is 2.1x against a 16% ROE, and trailing P/E is 12.75x, which sits inside the 10–18x utilities range. So I grade it fair, not cheap. It only looks deeply cheap against the broad market, which is not a fair comparison for a regulated power company. The main risk is heavy debt-funded capex: debt/equity is 0.82, FY26 free cash flow was -Rs 2,779 cr, and the government's newly announced offer-for-sale (OFS) adds supply pressure on the share price.

fundamental.thesis: IGL is the main city gas distributor in Delhi NCR, selling CNG to vehicles and piped gas (PNG) to homes and businesses. It is still adding volume: total volumes grew 6.9% YoY to 9.86 MMSCMD in H1 FY27, CNG rose 7.5% and domestic PNG rose 11.5%. Profits, however, have collapsed. H1 FY27 revenue grew 21.4% to ₹10,654 cr, but gas purchase costs jumped 39%, EBITDA margin fell from 12% to 3%, and PAT dropped 71% to ₹211 cr (a 2.0% margin). Q2 alone was much worse: EBITDA was negative ₹31 cr and PAT was about ₹26 cr, down roughly 93% from ₹386 cr a year earlier. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E, as suits a capital-intensive utility. On those, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 15.4x (inside the 10–18x utilities range), EV/EBITDA is 10.5x and the stock sits around the 12th–15th percentile of the market. But both figures are based on trailing earnings that are falling fast, and analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 50–59% in 90 days. So I grade it fair, and the low multiples may be a value trap. The biggest risk is that IGL cannot raise CNG and PNG prices to cover higher gas costs (in a politically sensitive Delhi market, with crude near $91 and rising), so margins stay crushed.

Tata Power is an integrated power company covering generation, transmission, distribution, renewables and solar manufacturing. That makes it a mix of steady regulated income and capacity-led growth, not a pure regulated annuity like NTPC or POWERGRID. On the extracted filings, Q2FY27 revenue was ₹19,636 cr, up 26.3% YoY, and PAT was ₹1,652 cr, up 32.6% (8.4% margin; the ₹59 cr exceptional gain is immaterial). Revenue growth has picked up from about +1% in Q3FY26 to +5.6% in Q1FY27 and +26.3% now. However, yfinance shows a much lower ₹12,877 cr for the same quarter, H1 EBITDA margin fell from 23.6% to 14.5%, and the FY26 row looks broken. So the speedup needs checking against the full consolidated PDF. For a capital-intensive utility, EV/EBITDA is the right yardstick. At 15.2x EV/EBITDA, 34.4x trailing P/E (sector band 10–18x) and 3.3x P/B on only 11.3% ROE, the stock costs well above the regulated utilities while earning a lower ROE. It only looks fair against the broad-market fallback peers, so I grade it expensive. The 23.6x forward P/E and 30-day estimate upgrades (+5.7%) mean strong growth is already priced in. The biggest risk is heavy capex funded by debt: debt/equity is 1.62x, H1 free cash flow was -₹3,696 cr, interest coverage is only 2.48x and the current ratio is 0.79. With a possible RBI rate hike, a slip in project execution or margins would hit the equity hard.

fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

Prestige Estates is a multi-city developer led by Bangalore, with projects in Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad and NCR, plus a growing rental and hospitality business. It is building scale by buying land aggressively: two 100%-stake acquisitions in November 2026 and ₹2,669 cr of land spend in H1 alone. Reported H1FY27 revenue was flat at ₹4,735 cr (-0.1% YoY) and PAT fell 31.4% to ₹528 cr, an 11.2% margin. Cash conversion stayed strong (CFO/PAT 2.48x, FCF ₹323 cr). The sector card says reported P&L lags the real business by 2-4 years, and the numbers that matter most for a developer (pre-sales, collections, net debt trend) are not in the data I was given, so I can't make a confident growth call. I used EV/EBITDA plus P/B-vs-ROE because P/E is not meaningful for developers. EV/EBITDA of 21.6x sits slightly below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P46), but P/B of 4.0x against an ROE of only 8% is rich, so overall valuation is fair. The 52-week position (60% of range) and the forward P/E falling to 26.5x from 55.2x trailing look neutral to mildly supportive. The biggest worry is leverage: debt/equity is about 1.05x while the company keeps buying land, and sell-side FY EPS estimates were cut 5.8% in 30 days and 8.2% in 90 days even though 19 of 21 analysts rate it a buy. That is a classic pattern before a stock gets re-rated lower.

fundamental.thesis: NTPC is India's largest power generator. Most of its earnings come from a regulated return (about 15.5% ROE) on the plants it has commissioned, with a fast-growing solar and renewables arm on top. H1 FY27 headline revenue was ₹100,262 cr, up 19.9% from ₹83,660 cr a year ago, but the company's core capacity-plus-energy billing grew a more modest 9.65%. Within that, capacity charges rose 6.7% to ₹35,909 cr, energy charges rose 11.6% to ₹55,845 cr and solar revenue rose 64.9% to ₹2,456 cr. Revenue growth has turned up from about -1.5% to -3% in FY26 to +7.0% in Q1 FY27 (PAT ₹6,896 cr, +12.9%, 13.6% margin), though H1 PAT was not extracted. For a capital-intensive utility I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, backed by P/B with ROE. On that basis it looks cheap against peers: EV/EBITDA is 8.4x against a peer median of 11.6x (cheapest in the peer group) and trailing P/E is 11.9x against 14.7x. P/B is 1.7x with ROE of 13.7%. It is only fair against the static 10–18x utilities P/E band. The forward P/E (12.8x) is above the trailing P/E, and this year's EPS estimates were trimmed 0.9% in the last 30 days, so near-term earnings look roughly flat. The main risk is earnings quality: CERC 2024 tariff orders are still pending, so bills are provisional and later adjusted (₹2,825 cr energy adjustment in H1), and large regulatory-deferral and deferred-tax swings make reported PAT hard to compare across periods.

fundamental.thesis: InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) is India's largest airline, with a 442-aircraft fleet, and its results are driven mainly by fares, fuel costs and the rupee rather than the order-book measures in the Industrials sector card. The biggest weakness is cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.31× PAT and free cash flow was -₹159 cr. Capex of ₹280 cr in H1 pushed net debt from ₹147 cr to ₹455 cr and finance costs rose 87%. Real leverage is still modest at roughly 0.18× equity; the 13.09 debt/equity figure in the snapshot is most likely a percentage, not a multiple.

EV/EBITDA of 14.0x is 35% below the peer median (P15), but one-off AbbVie income may be inflating EBITDA, so overall the grade is fair rather than cheap. fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Finance is India's largest diversified retail NBFC, with AUM of ₹5,84,624 cr and a customer franchise of 128.85 million. In Q2FY27, net total income grew 23% YoY to ₹15,974 cr and PAT grew 29% to ₹6,367 cr, while AUM growth picked up from 22.4% (Q4FY26) to 24% (Q1) to 26%, and GNPA improved to 1.06% from 1.24% a year ago. Note that the trend table's Q1FY27 and H1 'revenue' rows appear to use total income rather than net income, so I rely on the like-for-like Q2 net-income figures. Using the sector card's lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock trades at 4.93x book for a 17.9% TTM ROE (20.6% annualised in Q2), the most expensive P/B among its 10 credit-services peers (P100, +62% vs the 3.0x median) and P89 on P/E at 29.6x, so it is expensive even after allowing a quality premium. The 18.3x forward P/E and the 62% dividend yield look like data errors and are not relied on. The biggest risk is that management itself guides to modest NIM moderation with up to two more repo hikes to 6%, which turns the NBFC rate tailwind into a headwind. Stage 2 and 3 assets have also risen to 2.02% from 1.87%, and the ₹17,500 cr QIP plus promoter warrants will dilute ROE in the near term.

fundamental.thesis: Axis Bank is India's third-largest private-sector bank, with a large corporate and wholesale book, a growing retail franchise and a consolidated life-insurance associate (Axis Max Life). In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

fundamental.thesis: POWERGRID is India's dominant inter-state power transmission company, earning a regulated return on equity (about 15.5%) on assets it puts into service, so earnings depend on how fast new lines are commissioned rather than on power prices. Growth has been flat: H1 FY27 revenue rose 2.8% YoY to ₹23,313 cr and PAT rose 3.7% to ₹7,465 cr. The implied Q2 FY27 is revenue of ₹11,816 cr (about +2.9% YoY) and PAT of about ₹3,867 cr, a 32.7% margin, after Q1 grew revenue 2.7% with PAT down 0.9%. ₹18,913 cr of H1 capex should be commissioned over time and lift the asset base, but that has not shown up in reported growth yet. For a regulated utility I value it on P/B against ROE, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check. P/B of 2.64x for 16.5% TTM ROE (13.98% annualised H1) is fair, and both trailing P/E (14.2x, inside the 10–18x utilities range) and EV/EBITDA (10.7x) sit at the 25th percentile of peers (P25), only 3–7% below the sector median, so overall it is fair, not clearly cheap. A forward P/E slightly above trailing and 90-day EPS estimate cuts (-2.2% for this year, -3.3% for next) point to flat earnings, with the roughly 3–5% dividend yield as the main return floor. The biggest risk is that growth stays near 3% if new lines are commissioned slowly, while leverage stays high (debt/equity 1.42, ₹1.51L cr of borrowings) and free cash flow is slightly negative because of capex.

fundamental.thesis: SBI Life is a large listed Indian life insurer with a market cap of about ₹1.8L cr, and the sector card says to judge it on new business value (VNB), APE growth and price-to-embedded-value (P/EV), not PAT. H1 FY27 shows embedded value of ₹87,350 cr and six-month VNB of ₹3,270 cr, but no reliable growth rate can be calculated because the year-ago figures (₹7,600 cr and ₹275 cr) look like unit errors; the last usable revenue and PAT growth is Q1 FY27 at +16.9% and +21.9%, revenue growth has stayed in a +16% to +19% range rather than clearly slowing as the trend signal says, and the table mixes quarterly and cumulative periods. On P/EV, the stock trades at about 2.1x (₹1.8L cr / ₹87,350 cr), which I grade fair on a provisional basis because no peer or historical P/EV is provided; the 71.7x trailing P/E (peer median 53.7x) is not the right yardstick, and the 15% of 52-week range position offers a better entry only if growth holds, while the 15.0% dividend yield looks like a data error and is ignored. The main concern is business quality: 13-month persistency has slipped from 87.11% in H1 FY26 to 84.35% in Q1 FY27 and the expense ratio has risen from 10.9% to 12.05%, while FY EPS estimates have edged down about 1% over 90 days despite 34 of 35 analysts rating it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: ICICIPRULI (now ICICI Life Insurance) is one of India's largest private life insurers, with ₹3.29 lakh cr of assets under management, a 229.9% solvency ratio and a 99.3% claim-settlement ratio. New business has picked up after a flat FY26: in H1FY27, annualised premium equivalent (APE) grew +15.1% YoY to ₹4,935 cr (FY26 was only +2.2%), retail APE recovered from -0.1% to +9.9%, VNB grew +22.3% to ₹1,283 cr, and VNB margin widened to 26.0% from 24.7% in FY26. Gross premium grew +15.3% to ₹24,505 cr and PAT +26.5% to ₹760 cr, but PAT is not the right yardstick for a life insurer. On the life-insurer yardstick, price to embedded value (P/EV), the stock trades at about 1.24x (₹70,497 cr market cap vs ₹56,669 cr EV, which grew +12.2% YoY; FY26 return on EV was 11.9%), which looks cheap. Peer ranks agree: P25 on P/B and forward P/E, at a 22–25% discount to the peer median. The biggest risk is growth fading: management has guided that protection growth will cool from the 40–50% pace of the last four quarters, and Prudential's pending reclassification from promoter to investor could mean an overhang of stake sales, while the market is in a RISK_OFF regime.

fundamental.thesis: Ambuja Cements is the Adani group's cement arm and, together with UltraTech, holds about 45% of India's cement capacity, with 109 MT of cement capacity plus an announced expansion of about 30 MTPA. Results are getting worse: Q2FY27 revenue was ₹9,197 cr and PAT ₹236 cr, a 2.6% PAT margin, down from 6.1% in Q1FY27 and about 14% in FY26. H1FY27 revenue fell 3.8% YoY and H1 PAT fell 73.8%. EBITDA per tonne slipped to ₹770 against ₹887 in FY26 and below the ₹900–1,100 healthy band, because fuel cost rose to ₹1.87 per 1,000 kcal from ₹1.60 a year ago. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive cement, the stock trades at 18.5x, in line with the Materials peer median of 17.9x (P53). The cheap-looking 22x trailing P/E and 1.7x P/B are offset by an ROE of only 8.3% and a forward P/E of 26.9x that is above trailing, which implies earnings will fall, so we grade it fair, not cheap, despite sitting near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that sell-side EPS estimates keep falling (FY down 49% in 30 days and 68% in 90 days) while imported fuel stays high and the Penna/Sanghi plants run at only about 50% utilisation. The better trade mix (74% trade share, 37% premium share) and management's guidance of higher-single-digit to double-digit volume growth in H2 are the only offsets.

fundamental.thesis: Berger Paints is India's second-largest decorative paints maker, with growing industrial, construction-chemicals and international businesses; management says its market share held steady through Q2 despite the competitive shake-up caused by Birla Opus entering the market. Revenue growth has picked up from +0.4% in Q3 FY26 to +12.0% in Q1 FY27 and about +13.2% in Q2 FY27 (H1 FY27 revenue ₹6,784 cr, +12.5%; PAT ₹622 cr, +19.3%), but profitability is moving the other way: Q2 PAT, worked out from the H1 minus Q1 figures, was about ₹217 cr on ₹3,200 cr revenue (a 6.8% margin versus 11.3% in Q1), Q2 operating profit grew only 5.2%, H1 EBITDA margin fell to 14.4% from 17.0% in Q1, and H1 operating cash flow covered only 0.23x of PAT, with free cash flow at -₹82 cr. Judged the way the sector card says to judge paint companies (as consumer franchises on a 30-60x P/E band), a trailing P/E of 50.9x (38.7x forward) and EV/EBITDA of 30.9x put the stock at the upper end of fair. It ranks around P87 in the broad Materials peer set, but that set is mostly steel and metal names, and Berger still trades below its direct peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND; the stock sits mid-range at 48% of its 52-week band and sell-side estimate revisions are roughly flat over the last 30 days. The biggest risk is that raw-material costs keep rising (management sees no easing, and crude is climbing) while Birla Opus competes hard, which could keep squeezing margins even as volumes grow.

fundamental.thesis: Colgate-Palmolive India is the dominant oral-care franchise, with the number one toothpaste brand at roughly three times the size of the second player, 69-70% gross margins and an 81.6% ROE. Revenue growth has picked up from flat in FY26 to +9.0% in Q4FY26 and about +12% for the last two quarters, reaching Rs 1,706 cr (+12.4% YoY) in Q2FY27 on high-single-digit toothpaste volume growth, but PAT growth slowed from +10.6% to +4.3% (Rs 342 cr). PAT margin fell from 22.3% to 20.0% and EBITDA margin from 32.2% to 29.0% because ad spend rose 39.8% YoY to 18.4% of sales, while gross margin held flat. On the FMCG yardstick of P/E cross-checked with EV/EBITDA, trailing P/E of 41.1x sits at the low end of the 40-60x sector band and 6% below the peer median of 43.8x (P40), EV/EBITDA of 28.3x is at P20, and forward P/E of 34.1x implies earnings growth, so the stock grades fair with the price at 33% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that the heavy ad spending does not turn into lasting volume and premium-mix gains, leaving profit growth stuck in low single digits while revenue grows double digits.

fundamental.thesis: AU Small Finance Bank is a mid-sized retail and small-business lender, focused on vehicle loans and mortgages, that is awaiting final approval to become a universal bank. Q2 FY27 revenue growth accelerated from +18.7% to +25.7% YoY to Rs 3,590 cr, and PAT growth rose from +37.0% to +52.9% to Rs 858 cr, but PAT is up only about 3% from Rs 832 cr in Q4 FY26, so an easy prior-year base flatters the YoY figure; the trend table's 'contracting margin' signal looks like an artifact of mixed revenue definitions, as H1 revenue of Rs 12,374 cr is far above the Rs 6,974 cr sum of Q1 and Q2, while NIM slipped from 5.9% to 5.8%, CASA improved from 29.0% to 29.5%, and gross NPA improved from 2.1% to 1.99%. Using P/B plus ROE as the yardstick for lenders, the stock is expensive at 3.64x book against a 1.5x peer median (P100) with FY26 ROE of 14.2%, though the trailing P/E of 27.77x against a 16.8x median is also high, and stronger growth and a peer set that includes low-multiple PSU banks explain only part of the premium. The biggest risks are a slight worsening in net NPA (0.76% to 0.81%) and provision coverage (85% to 83%) at a price that leaves little room for error, plus the potential data leak reported on 2 November, since the bank's reply to the exchange was not available for review; the feed's 10% dividend yield and +24% target upside do not reconcile with the Rs 1 dividend and the roughly Rs 969 price implied by market cap, so neither was relied on.

Tata Chemicals sells soda ash, which makes it a global price taker, with plants in India, the US, the UK and Kenya; it also has a smaller consumer and specialty arm (Living Essentials, Rallis). EBITDA margin also slipped from 13.0% in Q1 to an implied ~9.2% in Q2, hurt by UK gas costs, the Kenya suspension and weak soda ash prices. There is no trailing P/E because profits are negative, so I graded on the sector card's yardstick for commodity chemicals (EV/EBITDA plus balance sheet). At 14.5x EV/EBITDA the stock costs roughly double the 5–8x mid-cycle norm, though that is partly because EBITDA is at a cyclical low. P/B of 0.82x is the cheapest in the sector (P0), so overall I call it fair, not a clear bargain. The main reason for caution is that analysts have cut this year's EPS forecasts by 55% in 90 days and their ratings lean sell (4 sell vs 2 buy).

fundamental.thesis: UTI AMC is one of India's older mutual fund houses, with a fee-based, asset-light model and no interest-bearing debt (net cash of about ₹273 cr). It earns mainly on equity AUM and flows, and also has pension, alternatives and international arms. H1FY27 revenue grew only 1.8% YoY to ₹983 cr, while PAT rose 10.4% to ₹426 cr; the PAT gain is mostly margin, not top-line growth. The quarter split is weaker: Q2FY27 alone works out to about ₹399 cr revenue (roughly -4.5% YoY, derived as H1 minus Q1) after Q1 grew +6.7%. The domestic business grew 3.8% while the international segment shrank 27.5%, so the 'accelerating' trajectory flag reflects lumpy treasury and other income more than a real AUM-led pickup. On valuation we did not have the AUM-linked earnings yardstick an AMC should be judged on (no AUM, flow or yield data), so we fell back to P/E and EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 30.5x, about 13% below the broad-market median and at the 42nd percentile; EV/EBITDA is 14.7x at the 25th percentile. With the stock near its 52-week low, this looks fair rather than clearly cheap for a slow-growing AMC. The biggest risk is that the company paid out 120% of profit as dividends and cash conversion was only 0.6x CFO/PAT in H1, which cannot last unless core fee growth picks up.

fundamental.thesis: Cochin Shipyard (COCHINSHIP) is India's largest PSU shipyard executing defence (Navy/Coast Guard) and commercial vessel contracts, backed by an order book of ₹21,100 cr (~5× annualised revenue) that provides multi-year execution visibility — structurally the most compelling asset on the balance sheet. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive model per the sector card, 45.51× sits at the upper bound of the 28–45× Industrials range and at P86 in the broad market (95% premium to median), grading expensive; the forward P/E discount (33.25× vs 54× trailing) signals the street is pricing in a sharp earnings recovery — but that recovery has not yet appeared in filed numbers and Q1 FY27 extraction is blank despite the August 2026 filing date. The single biggest risk is that margin compression deepens further on the ISRF ramp and rising crude-linked operating costs, in a RISK_OFF macro with D/E at 28.47 — any slippage in earnings recovery would unwind the current rich valuation quickly.

fundamental.thesis: GMR Airports is India's largest private airport operator, running Delhi, Hyderabad, Goa (Mopa), Medan, and newly Nagpur and Vizag. Its earnings depend on regulated aero tariffs plus a fast-growing non-aero business (retail, F&B, real estate, hotels). Revenue growth has slowed sharply: from +48.6% YoY in Q3FY26 to +23.0% in Q1FY27, and to about +11.6% in Q2FY27 (implied ₹4,188 cr, from H1 ₹8,273 cr minus Q1 ₹4,085 cr). EBITDA margin has slipped from 43.8% to 37.9% and passenger traffic grew only about 1%, so growth now rests on tariffs and non-aero income. Implied Q2 PAT is only about ₹65 cr (1.6% margin) after ₹1,931 cr of H1 interest, and yfinance shows a ₹15 cr loss, so profit quality is thin. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive, regulated-asset business and P/E is not meaningful: at 25.1x EV/EBITDA, 82.6x forward P/E (P98 among peers), negative book value and 98% of the 52-week range, it is expensive. The biggest risk is that weak traffic (Hyderabad -11.7%, Mopa -14.4%) plus a heavy debt load leaves the stock leaning on the Delhi CP-4 tariff being implemented on time.

fundamental.thesis: Graphite India makes graphite electrodes for electric-arc-furnace (EAF) steelmakers. It runs 80,000 tpa of capacity at 97% utilisation, and that demand depends on the steel cycle and on EAF adoption, not on an order book, so the Industrials order-book framework fits poorly. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose 34% YoY to Rs 1,871 cr and PAT rose 26% to Rs 265 cr; subtracting Q1 (Rs 842 cr / Rs 171 cr) implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 1,029 cr (+41% YoY vs Rs 729 cr) and PAT of about Rs 94 cr (+24% vs Rs 76 cr). However, the implied Q2 PAT margin fell sharply to about 9.1% from 20.3% in Q1, so revenue is accelerating while profitability per rupee is slipping. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, and the signals conflict, so the grade is fair: EV/EBITDA of 51x (P89, +119% vs median) and a trailing P/E of 72x look expensive because trailing earnings come from the FY26 trough (PAT -62%), while a forward P/E of 12.5x (P16), P/B of 2.2x, and a mid-range 52-week position price in a sharp earnings recovery that the 30-day sell-side EPS upgrade (+8.3%) supports. The main risk is that the recovery stalls as margins compress, global steel output stays flat (-0.2% YoY, China -1.6%), and Chinese electrode pricing pressure persists; the reported debt/equity of 6.27 also conflicts with the company's historically low leverage and is probably a units error, but it should be verified.

The biggest risk to this thesis is raw material cost volatility (nickel, ferro-alloys at ~70% of revenue) combined with structural Chinese overcapacity, which could further erode the already-contracting EBITDA margin (13.1% Q1FY27 vs 13.7% peak in FY26).

fundamental.thesis: Cohance Lifesciences is an Indian CDMO/API platform (formerly Suven Pharmaceuticals) serving global pharma innovators across Pharma CDMO, API+, Sapala nucleic-acid specialty chemicals, and Formulations — a niche franchise currently navigating a sharp operational trough driven by post-merger NJ Bio consolidation, Pharma CDMO order phasing, and Specialty Chemicals destocking. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue declined 23.1% YoY to ₹422 cr (decelerating sharply from +12.5% in Q1FY26 and extending the -13.1% full-year FY26 decline), with Pharma CDMO down 38.7% YoY, NJ Bio contributing an EBITDA loss of ₹328 mn, and PAT swinging to ₹-45 cr (-176% YoY); EBITDA margins imploded 2,220bps to 2.2%, though gross margins held at 71.5% and FCF remained a healthy ₹106 cr — indicating the trough is volume/timing-driven rather than structural margin destruction, and management has guided Q1FY27 as the floor with H2FY27 YoY recovery. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per sector card guidance for a capital-intensive CDMO, the stock trades at 39.3× (P81 vs broad-market peers, 68% premium to median 23.3×), expensive on any normalised basis; trailing P/E of 88.6× (P91, distorted by the trough PAT) and forward P/E of 38.9× still sit well above sector Pharma medians of 28–40×, while sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 25.5% in the last 30 days — suggesting the recovery the market is paying for is actively being revised downward. The biggest risk is binary: an active FDA Warning Letter at the Nacharam FDF facility, if not resolved swiftly, could trigger customer qualification audits across the CDMO business precisely when the recovery pipeline depends on securing and delivering new orders against a backdrop of dangerously high Debt/Equity of 9.93.

Rainbow Childrens Medicare runs a specialist chain of children's and women's hospitals: 26 hospitals with 1,910 operational beds out of 2,555 in total. About 65% of revenue comes from paediatrics, 63% of patients pay cash, and mature hospitals earn 73% of revenue at an ARPOB of about ₹66,900. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 23.2% YoY to ₹548 cr, up from +6.5% in Q2FY26 and +11.9% in Q3FY26, but PAT grew only about 11% to ₹84 cr. PAT margin has fallen from 17.0% to 15.3% and EBITDA margin from 33.5% to 31.0%, because the 5 new hospitals (12% of beds, 27.4% occupancy, -16% EBITDA margin) are still losing money and pulling the group's 49.2% occupancy down. For a capital-intensive hospital business I used EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick: at 26.1x it is only 12% above the broad-market median (P59) and within the usual range for Indian hospital chains, so valuation looks fair. Trailing P/E of 51.3x and P/B of 8.9x are rich, while a forward P/E of 36.5x assumes earnings growth. The biggest risk is that sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 3.6% over 30 days and 4.3% over 90 days even though all 14 analysts rate it a buy, which suggests margin dilution from new hospitals may last longer than the market expects.

fundamental.thesis: Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands is a mid-cap branded apparel company that owns Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Allen Solly and Peter England, plus a smaller emerging-brands portfolio. It sells through 3,434 stores, 40,500 multi-brand outlets, 6,800 shop-in-shops, e-commerce and wholesale. In Q2FY27, revenue grew 11.0% YoY to Rs 2,266 cr, up from +3.7% in Q2FY26 and +9.6% in Q3FY26, the fourth straight quarter of double-digit growth. PAT rose 126% to Rs 53 cr, but the PAT margin is still thin at 2.3%. EBITDA margin widened 60 bps to 17.2% and same-store (LTL) retail sales grew 5.3%, the 8th positive quarter in a row, though that is slower than before. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a store-heavy retailer, the stock trades at 15.9x versus a broad-market median of 23.3x (P28), and the forward P/E of 27x is far below the sector card's 60-100x range. The trailing P/E of 58x looks expensive only because current profits are low. I grade valuation fair, and the price sitting near its 52-week low gives a reasonable entry point. The main risk is profitability: net profit is only about 2% of revenue, and debt plus lease liabilities are high, so a weak festive season or slower same-store sales could wipe out much of the profit gain.

fundamental.thesis: Indiamart runs a large Indian B2B online marketplace, with 8.9 million supplier storefronts and 217 thousand paying suppliers, and earns mainly from advance-paid supplier subscriptions, which makes it a platform rather than a typical consumer company. Comparing like quarters (the pre-computed trend signals mix quarterly and full-year figures), Q2 FY27 revenue rose 9.7% YoY to Rs 429 cr, slowing from +12% a year earlier, while PAT rose about 10% to Rs 91 cr, EBITDA margin improved from 33% to 37%, and PAT margin stayed flat near 21%; however, paying suppliers fell 2% and collections grew only 9%, so growth depends on higher revenue per supplier rather than more customers, though cash conversion is strong at 1.48x CFO/PAT. Valuation is fair using a platform yardstick of EV/EBITDA and unit economics: EV/EBITDA of 18.1x and trailing P/E of 27.1x sit below the broad-market medians of 23.3x and 35.2x (no close peers are available), and cash of Rs 3,234 cr is about 25% of market cap, but trailing P/E rests on FY26 PAT of Rs 475 cr, while annualising the latest quarter gives about 35x, and the 20.7x forward P/E assumes a profit recovery that the Rs 91 cr quarter does not yet show. The biggest risk is that a shrinking paying-supplier base eventually limits pricing power and pulls revenue growth down toward or below the current 9% collections growth; the Rs 1,939 consensus target is also not relied on because its stated +23% upside conflicts with a price of about Rs 2,137 implied by the 52-week range.

Lemon Tree Hotels is India's largest mid-priced hotel chain, and it is shifting toward an asset-light model by splitting the hotel-owning business from the management and brand business (CCI, NSE and BSE have approved the scheme; NCLT sanction is still pending). H1 FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹706 cr, which works out to about ₹361 cr in Q2, up roughly 18% YoY, but growth across the trend window has slowed from +20.1% in FY25. EBITDA margin has held at about 44.5%, while reported H1 PAT of ₹89 cr (12.6% margin) is mixed up with large and inconsistently stated one-off items, and Q2 PAT by subtraction (about ₹32 cr) is below last year's roughly ₹35 cr. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hotel owner, the stock trades at 16.1x, 31% below the broad-market median (P29); trailing P/E is 39x and forward P/E is 22x. Near its 52-week low, that makes it fair to slightly cheap, but the leverage, the pending restructuring and steady small cuts to sell-side estimates (FY EPS -2% over 90 days) argue against a strong call.

fundamental.thesis: Swiggy is India's number-two food-delivery and quick-commerce (Instamart) platform, with a small but fast-growing out-of-home dining segment. Revenue keeps growing in the mid-30s: H1 FY27 rose 36.7% to ₹14,383 cr, and the implied Q2 is about ₹7,571 cr, up roughly 36% YoY, slower than FY26's +51.4%. The trend-table label 'accelerating' mixes half-year, full-year and quarterly periods and overstates the move. Losses are narrowing on a YoY basis: the H1 EBITDA loss fell to ₹997 cr from ₹1,606 cr and H1 net loss to ₹1,713 cr from ₹2,289 cr. Sequentially, however, the Q2 loss widened to about ₹922 cr from ₹791 cr in Q1. Food delivery is close to breakeven at a -7.65% margin, but Instamart still lost ₹1,415 cr at a -55.9% margin. Because P/E and EV/EBITDA are meaningless while the company is loss-making, I graded valuation on EV/sales plus unit-economics delivery, as the sector card prescribes for platforms. Price/sales of 2.89x (about 2.3x on annualised H1 revenue) and P/B of 3.35x (P37 vs the broad market) look fair, not stretched, for ~36% growth with improving margins. Sell-side estimates have been revised sharply upward (FY EPS +50.7% over 90 days), but there is no formal management guidance, and the main risk is that the Instamart cash burn in the quick-commerce price war delays group profitability.

fundamental.thesis: Exide Industries is India's leading lead-acid battery maker, serving automotive OEMs, the replacement market, inverters/solar, industrial and export customers, and it is building lithium-ion cell capacity through its subsidiary EESL, whose 6 GWh gigafactory was commissioned in September 2026. Growth has sped up sharply: revenue went from +4.1% in FY26 to +9.4% in Q4 FY26, +17.7% in Q1 FY27 and +18.9% for H1 FY27 (Rs 10,331 cr), while H1 PAT rose 46.7% to Rs 794 cr. Working back from the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 FY27 revenue was about Rs 4,803 cr (about +20% YoY) and PAT about Rs 443 cr (about 9.2% margin, up from 6.3% in Q1), helped by a 270 bps EBITDA margin expansion in Q2 and auto OEM sales growing 25%+ for a fourth straight quarter. I grade valuation on EV/EBITDA, the auto sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive names: at 18.6x it is close to the auto-parts peer median of 19.1x (P40), so the stock is fair; the 40x trailing P/E sits at P80 among peers and above the 18-28x ancillary range, but the 23.9x forward P/E prices in the earnings growth, and the stock already trades at 80% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the Rs 5,352 cr put into the lithium-ion business, which is holding ROE down at 6.2% until that plant scales profitably, alongside high lead and sulphur input costs and a tough comparison against last year's post-GST demand surge.

fundamental.thesis: Deepak Nitrite is an integrated Indian chemicals maker with a leading position in phenol and acetone (Phenolics), plus an Advanced Intermediates (AI) business serving agrochemical and other customers. Quarterly revenue growth has accelerated from +3.0% in Q3 FY26 and -3.0% in Q4 to +36.4% in Q1 FY27 and about +62% in Q2, while H1 FY27 revenue was Rs 5,654 cr (+49.0%) and PAT Rs 743 cr (+222%); Q2 is derived as H1 minus Q1 (revenue about Rs 3,076 cr, PAT about Rs 398 cr, margin about 12.9% vs 13.4% in Q1), and the gain leans on Phenolics, with H1 EBIT of Rs 933 cr, while AI margin fell to 7% from 10%. Using EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for chemical cyclicals, I grade valuation fair: the 24.6x headline (+37% vs the 17.9x peer median, P67) and 41.6x trailing P/E appear to use FY26 earnings, and my rough trailing-12-month estimates are about 14x EV/EBITDA and 22x P/E, which is below the headline but still above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle range on what may be peak earnings, while the 27.6x forward P/E implies PAT of only about Rs 830 cr, so either that figure is stale or earnings are expected to fall despite upward EPS revisions (the snapshot's dividend yield and implied price also look unreliable). The biggest risk is that Phenolics spreads normalise, as management itself signals with its 'new normal' language, just as the long-dated polycarbonate project (FY27 capex plan Rs 2,500 cr vs FY26 FCF of Rs 348 cr, commercialisation targeted by end FY2030) adds debt without near-term earnings.

fundamental.thesis: Apar Industries is a leading Indian maker of power-transmission conductors, specialty oils and cables, and it benefits directly from the grid-capex cycle. H1 FY27 revenue rose +25.0% YoY to ₹13,522 cr, and Q2 alone grew +21.3% to ₹6,931 cr. Revenue growth has held steady at +22% to +25% over the trend window. PAT jumped +77.7% to ₹915 cr, PAT margin widened from 4.8% to 6.8% and EBITDA margin from 9.2% to 11.8%. The conductor order book is a record ₹12,025 cr (+67% YoY) and Q2 order inflow rose +123%. Volume quality is weaker than the headline, though: conductor volumes fell 8% and oil volumes fell 17% in H1. So growth is coming mainly from higher prices (elevated metal and base-oil costs passed on) and a richer product mix, not more units sold. Valuation is expensive. Graded on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive names, it trades at 32.2x vs a peer median of 23.3x (P68). Trailing P/E is 59.2x, above the 28-45x Industrials band, at P77 on P/E and P90 on P/B. The stock sits at 90% of its 52-week range. The forward P/E of 46x and +21% upward revisions to FY EPS estimates offset this only partly. The biggest risk is earnings quality: H1 operating cash flow was -₹863 cr (CFO/PAT -0.94x) because of a ₹900+ cr inventory build and higher receivables, while US and export revenue are shrinking.

fundamental.thesis: BEML is a Schedule-'A' defence PSU under India's Ministry of Defence, manufacturing heavy equipment across mining, construction, defence platforms, and metro/rail segments, with revenue heavily dependent on government order execution. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹820 cr (+29.3% YoY from ₹634 cr) and the operating loss narrowed substantially (EBITDA swung from -₹41 cr to +₹3.6 cr YoY), yet PAT remained negative at -₹27 cr (-3.3% margin); more critically, FY26 full-year PAT collapsed 49.7% and order inflows landed at only ₹1,286 cr vs a ₹6,800 cr target — an 81% miss that is the single most important leading indicator for an order-book business. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial (Sector Card guidance), the stock trades at 48.4× (P88 among peers, 107% premium to sector median 23.3×) and trailing P/E of 94× versus the sector benchmark range of 28–45×, placing it firmly in expensive territory despite a more palatable forward P/E of 28× that already discounts a sharp earnings recovery. The biggest risk is that FY27 order inflows remain structurally below target, eroding book-to-revenue cover and triggering a 30–50% de-rating (consistent with Industrials sector card cycle-risk warning) before the earnings recovery the valuation demands actually materialises.

fundamental.thesis: Blue Dart Express is India's dominant integrated express logistics company and a DHL Group subsidiary, operating time-definite air and ground freight networks with significant pricing power in the premium segment. Q1FY27 showed a sharp positive inflection: revenue grew +15.0% YoY to ₹1,658 crore (accelerating from a flat +7% range across all FY26 quarters), while PAT surged 81.2% YoY to ₹88 crore with EBITDA margin expanding to 16.7% — the operating-leverage story is finally showing up in PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the preferred yardstick for capital-intensive logistics (EV/EBITDA is unavailable in the snapshot), the fallback trailing P/E of 40.4× sits within the Industrials sector range of 28–45× (fair), but forward P/E at 26.5× — below the 28× lower bound — implies the market is pricing in substantial earnings growth; the stock at 10.6% of its 52-week range (near ₹4,883 vs a 52-week high of ₹7,036) at a fair-to-cheap forward multiple presents a potentially asymmetric setup, though the falling-knife risk at this proximity to the low demands caution. The single biggest fundamental risk is that crude oil at $89.72 and rising directly compresses unit economics since freight and handling costs constitute 58% of revenues, and the 90-day EPS revision of -24.3% signals the sell side is already cutting numbers — a classic pre-derating pattern that could undermine the inflection narrative.

fundamental.thesis: Carborundum Universal is a mid-cap maker of abrasives, industrial ceramics and electrominerals, with a large standalone India business and overseas subsidiaries in Russia, Germany and South Africa. Revenue growth has picked up from about +2-4% YoY through FY26 to +17.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.1% in Q2FY27 (₹1,455 cr), and standalone revenue grew 28% on Ceramics (+36%). Reported Q2 PAT, however, fell 83% to ₹12 cr (0.9% margin) because of an ₹80 cr charge for closing the German subsidiary CAAG. Before exceptional items, profit (PBEBT) rose 22% to ₹138 cr, but Abrasives grew only 4% and Electrominerals profit fell 21%. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive Industrials name, the stock trades at 34.5x (P72 vs the broad market), and forward P/E is 40x (P82). The headline 115x P/E is inflated by the one-off charge. Against a 4.4% ROE and P/B of 5.8x, and with the price at 86% of its 52-week range, valuation looks expensive. Sell-side (4 sell, 2 hold) puts its mean target at roughly today's price. The biggest risk is the international subsidiaries: VAW in Russia is now on the US OFAC sanctions list, FZL in South Africa is being accounted for as not a going concern, and CAAG is winding down. Together they could bring more write-downs and keep weighing on reported earnings.

The single biggest risk is that ₹394 cr of loans artificially held in Stage II due to interim High Court orders could reclassify to Stage III NPA, compounding an already deteriorating GNPA trend and potentially triggering another provision surge that could cut PAT by a further 15–20%.

JSW Dulux (formerly Akzo Nobel India; JSW Group took control in Dec 2025) is a decorative and industrial paints maker that sold its Powder Coatings and IRC divisions and is now chasing market share. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,927 cr, up only 5.8% YoY as reported, but up 20% on a comparable retained-business basis with 23% volume growth, and the latest single quarter improved from Q1 FY27's -2.8%. Profitability is moving the wrong way: gross margin fell 1,180bp from 47.2% to 35.4%, EBITDA margin slipped to 13.2% from 14.4%, and PAT margin dropped to 7.8% from 12.1% on an operating basis, while cash conversion is weak (CFO/PAT 0.42x, FCF about ₹-8 cr). On valuation I used forward P/E and ignored the 7.45x trailing P/E, because the ₹1,874 cr one-off divestment gain inflates it; at 31.3x forward and 6.0x P/B the stock is cheap against the card's 60-100x discretionary norms, but analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (-5.8% over 90 days), so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that volume-led growth is being bought with price and margin under a new promoter, and the price increases do not restore gross margin before earnings estimates are cut further.

On valuation, the business is closest to a regulated utility, so I graded it on EV/EBITDA plus P/E: trailing P/E of 14.2x sits inside the 10–18x utilities band and EV/EBITDA is 7.4x. That makes it fair rather than cheap, because the broad-market peer discount ignores falling earnings and there are no city-gas peers in the comparison set. The biggest risk is that gas sourcing costs keep rising, for example through cuts in cheap government-allocated (APM) gas or a costlier spot-gas mix, faster than MGL can raise CNG and PNG prices, so margins keep compressing even as volumes grow.

fundamental.thesis: Hexaware is a mid-cap IT services firm reporting on a January–December year, with its strongest growth currently in Healthcare & Insurance (+31.9% YoY) and Manufacturing & Consumer (+31.1% YoY), while Travel & Transportation is shrinking (-14.5% YoY). In the latest quarter extracted from filings (Q2CY26, June quarter), revenue rose 17.9% YoY to ₹3,845 cr, but most of that came from the weaker rupee: constant-currency growth was 6.3%, up from 3.2% the quarter before. PAT fell 13% YoY to ₹330 cr, and PAT margin has slipped from 10.6% to 8.6% over the trend window, even though EBIT margin improved 352 bps YoY to 13.6%. On the IT yardstick (P/E backed by EV/EBITDA), trailing P/E is 21.8x, just under the 22–30x IT range, with forward P/E at 18.2x and EV/EBITDA at 13.0x, so I grade it fair: the discount is marginal, and sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 6.1% over 90 days, so the forward multiple may be too flattering. The biggest risk is that headline growth is mostly currency while PAT keeps shrinking under AI-driven pricing pressure. The September-quarter results filed on 2026-10-28 are not yet in the extracted data, so this view is one quarter stale.

fundamental.thesis: FACT is a PSU fertilizer producer (primarily complex fertilizers under the FACTAMFOS brand) operating as a near-monopoly in Kerala/South India, heavily dependent on government subsidy disbursements and imported raw materials — a price-taker in both inputs and outputs. Revenue recovered sharply to ₹1,484 cr in Q1 FY27 (+41.9% YoY, accelerating from the -24.9% trough of 9M FY2025), but this top-line bounce has not translated into operating profits: the fertilizer segment PBIT margin sits at -1.86%, the Q1 FY27 operating loss before finance costs was ₹36.51 cr, and the headline PAT of ₹3 cr (0.21% margin) is a statistical artefact of non-operating income rather than genuine operational recovery — full-year FY26 PAT was -₹40 cr. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per the sector card), FACT trades at 120.63× vs a fertilizer/chemicals cyclical mid-cycle norm of 5–8×, ranks P99 among 403 broad-market peers, and carries a P/B of 36.81× on a near-zero ROE — this is unambiguously expensive; the ₹50,886 cr market cap is disconnected from any demonstrated earnings power. The single largest risk is the compounding of a post-Q1 raw-material supply shock (West Asia geopolitical disruptions already causing plant shutdowns) on top of extreme financial leverage (D/E 295×) where quarterly finance costs of ₹61.98 cr structurally exceed operating income, leaving zero buffer for further stress.

fundamental.thesis: India Cements is a mid-sized South India cement maker with 14.75 MT of capacity (Q1FY26). It is now controlled by UltraTech, so the story depends on a turnaround under new ownership rather than on stand-alone strength. The latest extracted figures are stale: they run only to 9MFY26 (filed Jan-2026), and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-17 have not been indexed yet. In those older numbers, cumulative revenue growth picked up from -0.2% YoY in Q1FY26 to +4.8% in H1FY26 and +10.9% in 9MFY26 (₹3,256 cr). The company was still losing money, though the loss margin narrowed from -13.0% to -3.9% (9M PAT ₹-127 cr), while EBITDA margin slipped from 9.4% (H1) to 7.5% (9M), so the fall in costs per rupee of sales has not held. Because cement is capital-intensive, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 25.9× it sits well above normal cement multiples and above the broad-market median of 23.3×, and the 116× trailing P/E reflects barely positive earnings. The 1.06× P/B and the price near its 52-week low look cheap only on the surface. The 20.6× forward P/E already assumes a turnaround, while analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by about 21% in the last 30 days. Grade: expensive. The biggest risk is that EBITDA per tonne keeps lagging the healthy ₹900–1,100 band. Rising crude-linked fuel and freight costs and a risk-off market make that more likely, and the turnaround that today's price assumes would then be pushed back.

fundamental.thesis: SAIL is a large government-owned integrated steel maker, with Bhilai, Bokaro and Rourkela contributing about 81% of revenue, and it benefits from India's protected steel upcycle. H1 FY27 revenue rose 10.7% YoY to Rs 58,243 cr, improving from about +8% in H1 FY26, while EBITDA margin edged up from 10.9% to 11.5%; PAT jumped about 192% to Rs 3,395 cr, but EBITDA rose only about 14% (roughly Rs 840 cr against a PAT gain above Rs 2,200 cr), so the jump is not explained by operations, and the missing Q1 FY27 row means Q2 momentum cannot be isolated. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive steel, the 8.84x snapshot is slightly above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, while the 22.3x trailing P/E looks stale because filing-based trailing PAT of about Rs 5,516 cr implies about 13.6x, so I grade it fair: P/B of 1.3x with about 10.9% annualised ROE is not a clear bargain, the broad-market peer ranks are a weak comparison, and rising estimates (FY EPS +18.5% over 30 days) are offset by little upside, since the Rs 185 mean target is only about 2% above the roughly Rs 182 price implied by the 52-week position, not the stated 13.2%. The biggest risk is that the PAT surge proves non-recurring or steel spreads narrow, and no spread or EBITDA-per-tonne data was available to test this, with Rs 23,457 cr of provisionally priced government sales and a 0.79 current ratio adding balance-sheet risk.
