Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock looks expensive at 34.6× against the sector card's 5-8× mid-cycle range for chemical cyclicals and a 23.3× broad-market median (P73), with trailing P/E of 41.9× also above the 12-22× Materials range; there are no tight industry peers, and the feed's 27% dividend yield, 1.86 debt/equity and +54% target upside look wrong because the ₹494 mean target is only about 2.5% above the roughly ₹482 price implied by market cap. The biggest risk is a de-rating if growth stays flat, because forward P/E of 33× still assumes an earnings recovery while FY estimates have been cut by 10.7% over 90 days, with crude, monsoon and glyphosate-litigation risks adding pressure.

Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA, the better yardstick for a capital-intensive CDMO with negative earnings: the snapshot's 28.5x is P63 against a broad-market peer set, or roughly 22x on my estimate of trailing EBITDA, while trailing P/E is not meaningful, forward P/E of 37x is within the 28-40x pharma range, and the stock sits at 31.5% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that recovery depends on a stretched balance sheet, with H1 free cash flow of -₹468 cr and net debt of ₹5,097 cr; the reported 7.21x leverage appears to use unannualised H1 EBITDA, with about 4.2x being my trailing estimate, and the +8% consensus upside and 9% dividend yield look unreliable because the 52-week data and market cap imply a price near ₹160.

The margin trend is flat (Q1FY26 EBITDA margin was 21.0%, PAT margin 12.9%), and sell-side EPS estimates were raised 10% over 30 days and 20% over 90 days, which points to steady rather than explosive momentum. The biggest risk is that a ₹340 cr+ three-site capacity expansion and rising working-capital days land just as a risk-off, crude-inflated macro squeezes housing demand and gas-linked kiln costs.

fundamental.thesis: Urban Company is India's largest online platform for home services such as beauty, cleaning and repairs, and it also sells its own water purifiers and smart locks (Native), runs international operations and has a Saudi joint venture. It is now funding a heavily loss-making quick home-help business called InstaHelp. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹537 cr, up 41% YoY, faster than FY26's +36%. Orders rose 103% and Net Transaction Value (NTV, the total value of services booked) rose 39% to ₹1,432 cr. Profit went the other way: consolidated adjusted EBITDA was -₹144 cr, a -26.8% margin, against +6.8% for FY26. That is because InstaHelp lost ₹174 cr, which wiped out a core business that is profitable and improving (core EBITDA ₹30 cr, up 213% YoY; India consumer margin 3.5%, up 110 bps). Since the business is pre-profit, P/E means nothing here, so I graded valuation on price-to-sales and unit economics instead. At 12.3x sales and 8.6x book value (76th percentile of the broad market), the price is reasonable for 40% growth only if InstaHelp's losses keep shrinking. InstaHelp's loss per order did improve 19% from the previous quarter but is still ₹279. I rate valuation fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the InstaHelp cash burn continues while the newly approved ₹2,500 cr capital raise dilutes shareholders, in a risk-off market that punishes high-multiple loss-makers.

fundamental.thesis: JK Tyre is one of India's largest tyre makers, with 11 plants (9 in India, 2 in Mexico), about 38 million units a year of capacity, and a strong truck/bus and OEM franchise. EBITDA margin has roughly halved, from 13.3% in Q2FY26 to 7.1%, Q1 PAT fell 75% YoY to ₹44 cr (1.1% margin), and Q2 free cash flow was -₹447 cr. On the usual EV/EBITDA yardstick for a capital-intensive auto ancillary, the stock looks cheap at 7.7x EV/EBITDA and 14.6x trailing P/E against an Auto sector range of 18–28x (P6–P14 vs the market). However, those trailing multiples still include the high-margin quarters, analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 57% over 90 days, and annualised current-run-rate PAT would put the stock well above sector P/E, so we grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is further margin squeeze: about 70% of raw materials are petro-based, crude is above $102, debt is meaningful and cash flow is negative, so volume growth may not turn into earnings.

fundamental.thesis: CCL Products is one of the world's largest private-label instant coffee makers, with plants in India and Vietnam (Ngon Coffee, which earned ₹53 cr PAT in Q2 alone), plus a small but growing branded domestic business; it trades as FMCG but is mostly a B2B coffee processor exposed to green-coffee price swings. Revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +44.5% (H1FY26) and +38.5% (Q3FY26) to +13.7% in Q1FY27 and +10.5% for H1FY27 (₹2,411 cr). That implies Q2FY27 grew only about +7–8% (≈₹1,211 cr vs ≈₹1,127 cr), most likely as coffee-price pass-through fades. Profits are still growing much faster than sales: H1 PAT is up 42.5% to ₹247 cr, PAT margin has widened from 8.0% to 10.2%, and cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 1.78x, FCF ₹414 cr). Valuation is fair rather than cheap. I used EV/EBITDA because this is a capital- and working-capital-heavy processor, not a classic staples brand: EV/EBITDA is 21.6x (P46 vs market) and trailing P/E is 38.9x, at the bottom of the FMCG 40–60x band but rich for a commodity-linked exporter. Forward P/E of 24.1x already prices in strong earnings growth, and the stock sits at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps slowing toward single digits as coffee prices normalise, while margin gains, which drove most of this year's profit growth, become harder to repeat.

fundamental.thesis: SJVN is a government-owned regulated hydropower IPP (flagship 1,500 MW Nathpa Jhakri complex) expanding aggressively into renewables and thermal (Buxar 1,320 MW), earning a CERC-regulated ROE on commissioned capacity — earnings growth is therefore a function of commissioning pace, not power prices. Q1FY27 revenue surged +52% YoY to ₹1,394 cr driven by capacity additions, but PAT fell 1.2% to ₹225 cr as PAT margin compressed severely from 24.8% to 16.1% — a pattern that has deteriorated every quarter for six periods, with EBITDA margin also contracting from ~88% to 66%, reflecting rising interest burden on a highly leveraged balance sheet (D/E 2.25×, DSCR 0.60 — a 40% shortfall in debt servicing). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive regulated utility, at 15.88× SJVN sits within the regulated-utility peer range and at P28 vs broad market, while P/B at 1.86× (P16 vs peers) and forward P/E at 14× (P22 vs peers, deep discount to trailing 38×) reflect market pricing in earnings recovery — grading overall as fair, but the 52-week position at 12.8% of range and ongoing sell-side EPS cuts of -13.3% over 30 days caution against treating the cheapness as a catalyst. The DSCR of 0.60 combined with a current ratio of 0.54 means near-term liquidity is structurally stressed, and the NJHPS tariff determination pending since April 2024 (₹3,200+ cr billed provisionally under an expired 2019 tariff) creates a binary earnings event with no resolution timeline visible.

Solar Industries makes commercial explosives for coal miners such as CIL and SCCL, and it is now growing fast as a defence ammunition and energetics supplier. It sits under the Materials label, but it is really an explosives and defence business, so steel and chemical multiples do not apply. In the half-year to September 2026 (HY27, from the official filing), revenue grew +69.7% YoY to ₹7,187 cr and PAT grew +84.3% to ₹1,316 cr. That is faster than FY26 (+30.0% revenue) and Q3FY26 (+29.0%), and defence revenue more than doubled (+109% to ₹1,935 cr). EBITDA margin widened about 140 bps to 28.4%, so the pre-computed 'contracting' margin flag looks like a period-ordering artefact. The ₹20,178 cr order book (87% defence) covers roughly 2 years of revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business. At 65.8x EV/EBITDA, 101.7x trailing P/E and 32x P/B, the stock is at P93–P99 versus the broad market, well above the 12–22x Materials range and rich even for a defence name. The forward P/E of 63x and estimate upgrades (+11% FY-EPS over 90 days) show strong growth is already priced in, and the price is at 97% of its 52-week range. So: expensive. The biggest risk is that the defence order flow is lumpy and largely export-driven, so any slip in orders or execution would hit a stock priced for perfection.

fundamental.thesis: BSE is India's oldest stock exchange and a capital-markets infrastructure monopoly, earning revenues through transaction charges, listing fees, clearing/settlement, and investment income — it is not a traditional bank, so the relevant yardstick is P/E and EV/EBITDA (not P/B+ROE). At 48.1× trailing P/E (P68 vs broad peers) and EV/EBITDA of 28.4× (P63), the stock screens as fair against headline P/E metrics, but the forward P/E at 37.8× sits at P78 (expensive), P/B at 17.4× is at P94 (extremely elevated even for an asset-light exchange model), and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut sharply over the past 90 days (FY-EPS −6.6%, next-FY −9.8%) — a classic pre-derating signal that makes the 'fair' grade conditional on growth sustaining. The single biggest risk is that BSE's transaction-charge revenues are directly levered to equity market volumes and IPO activity, both of which face acute pressure from FII outflows of ₹44,000+ cr over 30 days, a RISK_OFF macro regime, and rising regulatory contribution costs (₹193 cr, +66% YoY), which could compress earnings faster than consensus currently models.

fundamental.thesis: CreditAccess Grameen is India's largest pure-play microfinance lender, with a gross loan book of about ₹29,294 cr that grew 21.5% YoY as of H1 FY27 and 2,276 branches lending mostly to rural women borrowers. That is roughly 7-8x the year-ago quarter, but off a provisioning-hit base, so the +691% H1 PAT and +144% revenue figures overstate the underlying growth, and the revenue figure also mixes NII with total income across periods. Asset quality is the real story: GNPA improved from 4.04% (9M FY26) to 3.17% (FY26) to 2.18% (Q1 FY27), with collection efficiency at 97.4% and provision coverage holding around 65%. Using the sector card's P/B-vs-ROE yardstick for lenders, a P/B of 2.91x against a TTM ROE of 16.4% (annualised H1 ROE about 24%) looks fair rather than cheap. The low forward P/E of 11x simply reflects the earnings normalisation, and analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by 9.8% in the last 30 days. The main risks are a fresh stress cycle in unsecured rural lending, a borrower count that is shrinking (-2.4% YoY) even as loan size grows, and a risk-off macro backdrop for a leveraged midcap lender.

fundamental.thesis: Indegene sells outsourced commercial, medical and regulatory content and technology services to global pharma companies, and it is a services business rather than a drug maker, with US revenue about 74% of the Q2 FY27 total (₹836 cr of ₹1,122 cr). Revenue growth accelerated from +14.8% in H1 FY26 to +23.6% in FY26, then held at +39.7% in Q1 FY27 and +39.5% in Q2 FY27 (₹1,122 cr), but profit has not kept pace: Q2 PAT rose only 10.0% to ₹112 cr, H1 PAT rose 4.6%, H1 PAT margin fell from 14.0% to 10.3%, Q2 EBITDA margin slipped to 16.7% from 19.1% in Q1, and H1 operating cash flow was about -₹1 cr against FY26's healthy 1.62x CFO/PAT. Earnings conversion is the biggest thesis risk, and two snapshot figures look unreliable: the 4.6 debt/equity is probably a percentage given about ₹100 cr of net cash, and the consensus +12% upside conflicts with a price near ₹519 implied by the 52-week position, so the target gets little weight.

Vijaya Diagnostic is a consumer-facing diagnostics chain with 168 centres across 27 cities. About 92% of revenue comes from individual patients (B2C), and it leads its home market of Hyderabad, which makes up about 67% of revenue. Growth is speeding up: revenue growth went from +14.9% in H1 FY26 to +19.5% in FY26 and +24.8% in H1 FY27 (₹486 cr). Q2 FY27, worked out as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹255 cr (+26% YoY) with PAT of about ₹60 cr, and H1 PAT grew +37.5% while EBITDA margin rose 357 bps to 43.4% and cash conversion stayed strong (FY26 CFO/PAT 1.56x). The sector card has no diagnostics yardstick, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E. The stock is expensive: trailing P/E of 82.8x against a healthcare band of 28–40x, EV/EBITDA of 41.9x, the 83rd–94th percentile of the broad market on every multiple, and a price at 90% of its 52-week range. The consensus target is only about 8% above the price, so most of the strong delivery already looks priced in. The biggest risk is that this rich multiple depends on new hubs in Bengaluru, Kolkata and the North-East ramping up on time, while finance costs rose 46% YoY and Hyderabad still dominates revenue.

Valuation is expensive using the pre-profit yardstick of EV/sales proxied by P/S, growth delivery and unit economics rather than trailing P/E: P/S is 15.5x (about 11x annualised Q2 revenue), forward P/E is 374x, and the stock is near its 52-week high with the mean target about level with the price, though EV/EBITDA is not meaningful, no tight peer set is available, and the price inputs and 25.82 debt/equity figure look inconsistent or unclear and were given little weight. The biggest risk is that aluminium, copper and memory-chip cost inflation interrupts margin gains while share is falling, a concern supported by next-FY EPS estimates being cut 49% in 30 days even as all 12 analysts stay at buy.

Asahi India Glass is India's leading automotive glass supplier and also has a growing float (architectural) glass business; in H1 FY27, auto glass made ₹2,015 cr of revenue and float glass ₹1,153 cr. Growth is speeding up. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹2,999 cr (+26.0% YoY) and PAT was ₹316 cr (+179.8%). Taking H1 minus Q1 gives an implied Q2 of about ₹1,586 cr revenue (+36.5% vs ₹1,162 cr) and ₹167 cr PAT (+188% vs ₹58 cr), so quarterly revenue growth went from -0.1% to +15% to about +36%. PAT margin roughly doubled from 4.7–5.0% to 10.5%, and EBITDA margin rose from 16.9% to 22.4%, with float glass the standout (+49.7% growth, 22% PBIT margin). Because this is a capital-intensive business, I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA. At 25.0x it is only 7% above the broad-market median (P55), which makes it fair. The P/E numbers look stretched, though: trailing 55.7x and forward 41.8x (P84) are well above the 18–30x auto norm, and even the annualised H1 run-rate is about 39x. Much of the PAT jump is a base effect against a weak FY26, so the price already assumes the recovery lasts.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Elxsi is a Tata Group engineering R&D services company specialising in embedded systems design for automotive, media & entertainment, and healthcare verticals — a niche deep-tech services player distinct from commodity IT outsourcers, with a strong domestic and global client base in high-complexity design programmes. Revenue growth has inflected sharply from a -3.9% trough in Q2FY26 to +14.7% YoY in H1FY27 (₹2,077 cr), with PAT rising +13.9% to ₹341 cr and PAT margin holding steady at 16.4%; the System Integration segment contributed 28.9% YoY growth, signalling service diversification — however, EBITDA margin has contracted ~290 bps from its peak of 28.1% (Q3FY26) to 25.2% (H1FY27), driven by New Labour Code wage provisions and rising employee benefits costs. Trailing P/E of 40.78× is above the IT sector benchmark upper bound of 30× (expensive on that metric alone), but the forward P/E collapses to 26.22× — within the 22–30× sector range, confirming earnings recovery is priced in — and peer-rank analysis places TATAELXSI at P60 on both trailing and forward P/E (fairly valued per the ≥P75 expensive threshold); at 6.7% of its 52-week range the stock appears sentiment-oversold relative to an improving earnings trajectory, consistent with the FY26 exceptional charge now cycling out of the base. The primary risk is sustained EBITDA margin compression from structural wage inflation and New Labour Code costs, amplified by a persistent negative EPS revision trend (-0.9% over 90 days, -1.2% next-FY) that historically flags further analyst downgrades ahead, and a long-run AI-driven structural threat to engineering services demand that the sector card explicitly flags as unproven in revenue terms.

C.E. Info Systems (MapmyIndia) is India's leading digital maps and location-intelligence company, selling map data, APIs and IoT/telematics devices to auto makers, enterprises and government. H1FY27 revenue grew +15.3% YoY to ₹271.5 cr, up from roughly +2-3% through FY26, and consolidated PAT rose +32.1% to ₹85.0 cr; Q2 alone works out to about ₹131 cr of revenue (about +16% YoY) and ₹35 cr of PAT (H1 minus Q1). The growth quality is weak, though: almost all of it came from the device segment (+161% to ₹56.2 cr), while the core map data and services business, about 79% of revenue, grew just +0.7%, and the PAT margin fell to about 27% in Q2 from 35.6% in Q1. On the IT yardstick of P/E, the trailing 36.9x sits above the 22-30x sector band, but forward P/E of 22.5x falls inside it and the stock ranks in the middle of the broad-market peer set (P53 on P/E, P64 on EV/EBITDA at 29.1x), so I grade it fair rather than cheap, even though it trades near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that the high-margin core map business has stalled while sell-side EPS estimates keep falling (-3.0% FY over 90 days, -4.1% next-FY), so the low price may be a falling knife rather than a value entry.

fundamental.thesis: Chennai Petroleum is a standalone refiner and IOC subsidiary, so its earnings track gross refining margins (GRM, the profit per barrel of crude processed) rather than administered retail fuel prices. Taking the official H1FY27 filing (₹51,414 cr revenue, ₹3,278 cr PAT) and subtracting Q1 gives an implied Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹22,055 cr, up roughly 10% YoY. That is a sharp slowdown from +57% in Q1, so the pre-computed 'accelerating' label is misleading because it mixes half-year and quarterly periods. Implied Q2 PAT was ₹2,247 cr, a 10.2% margin, driven by GRM rising to $8.78/bbl from $3.22 a year ago and a ₹385 cr one-off retrospective price adjustment, even though crude throughput fell 4.5%. On live ratios the stock looks cheap, using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-intensive refiner: trailing P/E 5.4x, EV/EBITDA 3.8x and P/B 1.5x against a 32% ROE, all bottom-percentile versus the market and below the 8–14x energy band. However, these are peak-cycle refining margins, and next-year EPS estimates were cut 11.6% in the last 30 days, so normalised earnings likely put it closer to fair. The bigger worry is earnings quality: H1 operating cash flow was only ₹25 cr against ₹3,278 cr of profit (0.01x), receivables jumped from ₹235 cr to ₹2,008 cr, cash fell to near zero after dividends, and the auditor flagged board-composition non-compliance.

Authum Investment & Infrastructure is a midcap NBFC and investment holding company. A large part of its earnings comes from investment and treasury income and from distressed-asset acquisitions; the latest is an NCLT-approved resolution plan announced on 2026-10-28. Its earnings are not steady lending income. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 12.6% YoY to ₹685 cr, but PAT fell 45.5% YoY to ₹418 cr. PAT margin dropped to 61.0%, from 74.6% in Q1FY27 and 71.0% for H1FY27. Revenue growth slowed from +21.4% in Q1 to +12.6% in Q2, and H1 PAT is down 10.6%. Cash backing for profits is weak: H1FY27 operating cash flow was -0.49x PAT and free cash flow was -₹763 cr. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for lenders, not P/E. P/B of 2.91x with ROE of 13.1% is roughly fair, since the stock is neither under 1.5x nor above 3x with sub-12% ROE. The headline P/E of 8.95x sits at P5 of the broad market, but it is flattered by lumpy investment gains and should not be read as cheap. The main risk is that profits depend on market-linked and one-off gains that are not turning into cash. Thin lender disclosures (no NIM or GNPA data) and the reported 24.6 debt/equity also need checking against the filings.

PAT was about ₹757 cr, up about 17.7% YoY, and PAT margin has held flat near 23%. Under the surface, net interest income grew only 9.8% YoY against 24-25% loan growth, NIM slipped from 3.5% to 3.36%, credit cost rose to 0.52% in Q1FY27 from 0.15% in FY26, and capital adequacy fell from 26.1% to 21.2% as the book grew faster than equity. Using the lender yardstick the sector card asks for (price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E), a P/B of 3.19x for an ROE of only about 12-12.6% is expensive, even though it sits around the 36th-38th percentile against the broad market and the forward P/E of 19.9x implies expected earnings growth. The biggest risk is that loan growth keeps outrunning lending spreads and capital, while the CFO's resignation on 2026-10-23 adds governance and continuity uncertainty for a midcap lender running debt-to-equity near 4.9x.

fundamental.thesis: CAMS is India's largest mutual-fund registrar and transfer agent (RTA). It is an asset-light business that earns fees linked to mutual-fund AUM, which makes it a direct beneficiary of household savings moving into financial assets. Revenue growth recovered from +3.2% YoY in Q2FY26 to +11.5% in Q1FY27, then eased slightly to +10.0% (Rs 414 cr) in Q2FY27. PAT grew faster than revenue, up 14.4% YoY to Rs 131 cr, with PAT margin around 31-32% and EBITDA margin around 46-48%. H1FY27 earnings were cash-backed (CFO/PAT 0.98x, Rs 819 cr net cash). I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA, since earnings track AUM, not on P/B: the 15.6x P/B reflects a 38.7% ROE, not a high price. The trailing P/E of 43.6x is about 24% above the market median, and EV/EBITDA of 27.6x is around the 60th percentile. Forward P/E of 32.2x implies continued earnings growth. With a premium capital-markets franchise and the stock at 84% of its 52-week range, I call it fair, not cheap. The main risk is that AUM growth slowed from 16.0% to 12.1% YoY, and sell-side EPS estimates were cut about 3% over 30-90 days even though all 18 analysts rate it a buy, which is a classic setup for a de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Suzlon is India's largest domestic wind turbine maker, with a 6.1 GW order book (84% from PSU and commercial/industrial buyers). PAT fell -5.9% to ₹305 cr, PAT margin dropped from 10.4% to 8.0%, and EBITDA margin dropped 360 bps to 15.6%. Execution growth also slowed to +14%, and the order book covers only about 2x revenue, well short of the 3x+ that would give strong visibility. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is an order-book industrial. At 25.7x it is about 10% above the broad-market median (P58), so it is fair, not cheap. The 25.3x trailing P/E looks low against the 28–45x Industrials range, but FY26 PAT (19% margin, including a ₹1,114 cr Q4) looks inflated by one-off tax credits, which also distorts the 40.6% ROE and 10.2x P/B. The 5.87 debt/equity figure looks inconsistent with Suzlon's historically low-debt balance sheet and should be treated as suspect data. The biggest risk is that margins keep compressing while earnings fail to turn into cash (CFO/PAT 0.38x in FY26). Analysts cut FY EPS estimates 10.6% over 90 days, and Q2 results are due on 29 Oct.

fundamental.thesis: TARIL is a mid-cap power transformer and rectifier manufacturer directly exposed to India's ₹9 lakh cr T&D build cycle, with execution growth of 23.7% in the most recent sector KPI read, positioned at an early stage of the structural capex upcycle. H1FY27 results (official NSE filing 2026-10-13) show revenue +32.6% YoY to ₹1,312 cr and PAT +39.0% YoY to ₹146 cr at an 11.1% PAT margin — a solid recovery vs Q1FY27's softer +8.1% standalone growth — but cash flow quality has deteriorated sharply to 0.33x CFO/PAT (from 0.84x in the prior comparable period), with ₹107 cr inventory build and net debt rising 24.7% HoH to ₹559 cr, flagging heavy working-capital absorption. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per sector card), TARIL trades at 23.3× — exactly at the P50 peer percentile and sector median — while trailing P/E of 32.6× sits at the lower end of the 28–45× Industrials range and the stock sits at 20.1% of its 52-week range; verdict is fairly valued with modest risk/reward support from the depressed price level. The primary risk to the thesis is that sustained weak cash conversion combined with a 24.7% HoH rise in net debt leaves minimal self-funding capacity, and any slowdown in order execution or lengthening of customer payment cycles could rapidly escalate balance sheet pressure on a business already running at 1.46x net debt/EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: IRFC is the Government of India's dedicated financing arm for Indian Railways (82.9% government-owned after the June 2026 OFS). It mainly leases rolling stock and project assets to the Ministry of Railways, so credit risk is quasi-sovereign and gross and net NPA have been 0.0% for every reported period. Revenue is growing fast and the pace is picking up: up 22.8% YoY to ₹16,316 cr in H1FY27, against +0.5% in FY26 and -2.4% in 9M FY26. Implied Q2 revenue is about ₹8,055 cr (+26% YoY). Profit is not keeping pace, though. H1 PAT rose only 10.3% to ₹3,886 cr, the PAT margin slipped from 26.5% to 23.8%, and NIM eased from 1.55% to 1.48%, so earnings are rising more slowly than the loan book. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, which is the right yardstick for a lender, not P/E. At 2.3x book for a 12.8–13.3% ROE and roughly 1.4% ROA, the stock is fair, maybe slightly full, for a low-margin, policy-driven financier.
